Q1. Definition of physiotherapy? Explain in detail the principles of evidence based practice in physiotherapy?

Full answer →

Define physiotherapy, then explain the EBP triad and the five EBP steps with a physiotherapy example and the evidence hierarchy.

  • Marks plan: definition of physiotherapy (1.5), EBP triad from Sackett (1.5), the five steps with a physiotherapy example (3), hierarchy of evidence (2), application in practice + conclusion (2).
  • Must include: a proper definition AND the five EBP steps with an example — students who write only the definition lose 5 of the 10 marks.
  • Bonus: naming PEDro as the physiotherapy-specific database earns a bonus smile.
  • Definition (World Physiotherapy): physiotherapy is the service provided only by, or under the direction and supervision of, physiotherapists.
  • It helps individuals and populations develop, maintain and restore maximum movement and functional ability throughout the lifespan.
  • It is needed where movement and function are threatened by ageing, injury, disease or environmental factors.
  • Physiotherapy is a primary-contact, autonomous profession and works within the ICF framework.
  • EBP (Sackett): the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of the best current research evidence.
  • EBP combines three things (the triad): best research evidence + the clinician's expertise + the patient's values and circumstances.
  • All three legs are needed — remove any one and the practice is no longer evidence-based.
  • Evidence without expertise is cook-book medicine; expertise without evidence is just opinion.
  • Evidence and expertise without patient values is paternalism.
  • Step 1 — Ask: convert the clinical problem into a focused, answerable PICOT/PICO question.
  • PICO example: "In chronic low-back pain (P), is motor-control exercise (I) more effective than general exercise (C) for reducing disability (O) at 3 months (T)?"
  • Step 2 — Acquire: search the literature systematically using PubMed/MEDLINE, PEDro (physiotherapy-specific) and the Cochrane Library.
  • Use MeSH terms and Boolean operators while searching.
  • Step 3 — Appraise: judge each study for validity, magnitude and applicability.
  • Use the hierarchy of evidence: systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs at the top.
  • Below them come RCTs, then cohort, then case-control, then cross-sectional, then case series, and expert opinion at the bottom.
  • Step 4 — Apply: integrate the appraised evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's preferences, culture and finances.
  • This matters in Indian practice — e.g. the cost of shockwave therapy for a daily-wage patient.
  • Step 5 — Assess (audit): evaluate the outcome of the decision and your own performance; this feeds the next cycle.
  • Reproduce the 5-step EBP cycle diagram and the evidence pyramid in any EBP answer.

EBP = E′·E′·P′ — Evidence + Expertise + Patient values (three legs of one stool). The five steps are the five A's in order: Ask → Acquire → Appraise → Apply → Assess.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 1 (a, d).
  • Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM. Churchill Livingstone (syllabus Paper-I reference 5).
  • Herbert R, Jamtvedt G, Hagen K, Mead J. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy. Churchill Livingstone (syllabus Paper-I reference 6).
  • World Physiotherapy policy statement — description of physiotherapy.
210 marks

Q2. Write the ethical issues faced in clinical practice of physiotherapy?

Full answer →

State the four principles of biomedical ethics, then explain at least six real ethical issues with an Indian clinical example each, plus ICMR rules and how to resolve them.

  • Marks plan: four cardinal principles of biomedical ethics (2), at least six ethical issues explained (4.5), research/ICMR issues (1.5), resolution strategies + conclusion (2).
  • Marks come from explaining each issue with an Indian clinical example — not from listing single words.
  • An answer without the four principles and without an ICMR mention rarely crosses 6.
  • Four principles of biomedical ethics (Beauchamp & Childress): autonomy — respect the patient's informed choices.
  • Beneficence — act in the patient's best interest.
  • Non-maleficence — do no harm.
  • Justice — fair, equitable distribution of services.
  • The syllabus also adds the World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice and the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines as the profession's normative documents.
  • Issue 1 — Consent and autonomy: treating without adequate explanation; in India families often decide for the patient, so negotiating informed consent across language and literacy barriers is a daily issue.
  • Issue 2 — Confidentiality: sensitive conditions (HIV status, occupational injury claims) shared casually in open treatment areas or with employers without consent.
  • Issue 3 — Scope of practice & referral: treating beyond competence (e.g. manipulating the cervical spine without training), or handling red-flag cases that needed medical referral.
  • Issue 4 — Overtreatment & commercial pressure: unnecessarily prolonged packages; outcome-driven billing exploits the imbalance of knowledge.
  • Issue 5 — Dual relationships/boundaries: treating relatives or close acquaintances, gifts, or social-media friendships that cloud clinical judgement.
  • Issue 6 — Documentation & record keeping: poor notes that fail medicolegal scrutiny; tele-rehabilitation consent and data privacy.
  • Issue 7 — Equity: refusing treatment to patients with infectious disease; gender-related discomfort (female patients and male therapists in India and vice versa); access for the poor.
  • Issue 8 — Advertising & misrepresentation: promising cures ("guaranteed back-pain relief") violates honesty.
  • Research ethics link: ICMR 2017 guidelines and RIPE 2020 require institutional ethics-committee approval, voluntary participation and compensation for trial injury.
  • This applies directly to any postgraduate dissertation involving patients.
  • Resolution: institutional ethics committees, professional codes (World Physiotherapy/IAP), continuing education, peer review, honest documentation and transparent billing.
  • The ethical clinician builds these into the system rather than relying on good intentions.
  • Reproduce the four-principles quadrant diagram with patient welfare at the centre.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 2 (a–d).
  • ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research involving Human Participants, 2017 (syllabus Paper-I reference 9).
  • World Physiotherapy (2011) Standards of Physical Therapy Practice (reference 8).
  • Beauchamp TL, Childress JF. Principles of Biomedical Ethics. (standard ethics reference)
310 marks

Q3. Importance of pilot study in clinical research?

Full answer →

Define a pilot study, give its five purposes (feasibility, protocol, instruments, sample size, resources), a physiotherapy example, and its limitations.

  • Marks plan: definition of pilot study (1), the five purposes at 1 mark each (5), an illustrative physiotherapy example (2.5), limitations & reporting (1.5).
  • One sentence examiners hunt for: "a pilot study tests the research process, not the hypothesis."
  • Follow that sentence with the five purposes and a dissertation-style example.
  • Definition: a pilot study is a small-scale preliminary version of the main study.
  • It is run on a handful of participants — often about 10% of the intended sample.
  • Its job is to test whether the full study is feasible — NOT to test the hypothesis itself.
  • Purpose 1 — Feasibility of recruitment: can we actually enrol 40 knee-OA patients in 3 months from one OPD? Are the inclusion criteria workable?
  • Purpose 2 — Protocol refinement: tests the intervention — dosage, session length, timing of outcomes; reveals impractical procedures (e.g. a 90-minute assessment no patient completes).
  • Purpose 3 — Instrument testing: checks whether the outcome measures are understood — e.g. does the translated SPADI read naturally for Kannada-speaking patients? Look at missing-item rates and floor/ceiling effects.
  • Purpose 4 — Sample-size estimation: gives pilot variance (SD) values to feed the power calculation for the main trial.
  • Purpose 5 — Resources, cost & data management: estimates drop-out rate, staff time and budget, and whether the case-report form/eCRF actually captures the data.
  • Example: before an RCT of eccentric vs concentric quadriceps training in patellofemoral pain, a pilot with 8 patients showed that the VAS diary confused participants and that two dropped out due to travel cost.
  • The main study then switched to a numeric pain rating at weekly visits and offered transport reimbursement.
  • Limitation: small samples cannot confirm the main effect — estimates are unstable, so the main study may still fail.
  • Limitation: pilot data must NOT be pooled into the main analysis.
  • Reporting: findings must be reported as feasibility outcomes (Lancet 2016 extension guidelines for pilot trials).
  • Reproduce the pilot-to-main-study flow diagram with the five purpose branches.

Pilot study: tests the process, never the hypothesis — "P for Process, not Proof".

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 3a (iii–vi).
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research. 4th ed. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins (syllabus Paper-I reference 11).
  • Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics. 4th ed. CRC Press (reference 12).
410 marks

Q4. How would you differentiate between simple random sampling and complex random sampling designs? Explain clearly by giving examples?

Full answer →

Define simple random sampling, then contrast it with the complex designs (stratified, cluster, systematic, multi-stage) using numbered examples and a comparison table.

  • Marks plan: simple random sampling — definition, methods, merits/demerits (2.5), stratified with example (2), cluster with example (1.5), systematic & multi-stage with example (2), comparison summary table (2).
  • The differentiator marks sit in the examples with numbers — "every 5th patient," "6 of 40 colleges."
  • State clearly that stratified samples within strata are still random — students often mistake stratification for quota sampling (which is non-probability).
  • Simple random sampling (SRS): every member of the sampling frame has an equal and independent chance of selection.
  • Methods: lottery, random number tables, or computer-generated random numbers.
  • SRS is the only purely probability-based design and needs no knowledge of the population's structure.
  • But SRS demands a complete sampling frame and spreads samples thinly across wide areas.
  • SRS example: drawing 60 of 400 registered low-back-pain patients from a hospital list using random numbers.
  • Complex (restricted) random designs are: stratified, cluster, systematic and multi-stage.
  • Stratified: first divide the population into homogeneous strata (by sex, disease severity, age band), then do SRS within each stratum, often proportionally.
  • Stratified guarantees representation of small subgroups and improves precision.
  • Stratified example: in a TKR study, sample male and female patients separately in a 1:2 ratio because the clinic population is one-third women.
  • Cluster: randomly select natural groups (schools, villages, wards) and study all members of the chosen clusters.
  • Cluster is cheapest for dispersed populations but less precise (intra-cluster correlation).
  • Cluster example: randomly pick 6 of Bengaluru's 40 physiotherapy colleges and survey every final-year student in them.
  • Systematic: pick every k-th person from a list after a random start, where k = frame size ÷ sample size.
  • Systematic is simple but has a risk of periodicity.
  • Systematic example: every 5th patient attending an OPD from a random Monday start.
  • Multi-stage: random selection in successive stages (state → district → hospital → patient), practical for large community surveys.
  • Multi-stage example: Karnataka → 4 districts → 2 PHCs each → all adults screened for knee OA.
  • Comparison table — frame needed: SRS needs a complete list of all; complex designs need only a list of strata/clusters.
  • Comparison table — precision: SRS is the baseline; stratified is higher, cluster is lower.
  • Comparison table — subgroup representation: chance-dependent in SRS; stratified guarantees it.
  • Comparison table — cost/logistics: high for dispersed populations in SRS; cluster/multi-stage are cheapest.
  • Reproduce the sampling-designs tree diagram (one trunk, four random branches).

Sampling ladder: Systematic = every k-th from a list; Stratified = strata first, random inside each; Cluster = whole groups at random.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 3a-iv.
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research. 4th ed. (reference 11).
  • Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics. 4th ed. (reference 12).
510 marks

Q5. Write in detail the fundamentals of qualitative research methods?

Full answer →

Explain the qualitative paradigm, name the major designs, describe sampling and data collection, analysis, and the trustworthiness criteria.

  • Marks plan: paradigm & when qualitative methods are appropriate (1.5), major designs (2.5), sampling & data collection (2.5), analysis approaches (2), trustworthiness criteria (1.5).
  • Viva trap: qualitative research is NOT "research without numbers because it's easier" — it is a deliberate paradigm with its own rigour.
  • Score by naming two designs AND two trustworthiness criteria with their quantitative equivalents.
  • Paradigm: qualitative research explores meanings, experiences and processes — the "why" and "how" — rather than measuring quantities ("how much").
  • It answers questions RCTs cannot: e.g. how do stroke survivors in rural Karnataka experience self-management?
  • Data are words and observations, and the researcher is the instrument.
  • Design — Phenomenology: the lived experience of a phenomenon (patients' experience of chronic low-back pain).
  • Design — Grounded theory: builds a theory from data through constant comparison, to explain a process (how adherence to home programmes develops).
  • Design — Ethnography: the culture of a group (pain beliefs within a community).
  • Design — Narrative inquiry / case study: stories of illness over time.
  • Sampling: purposive sampling of information-rich cases, extended by the snowball technique.
  • Enrolment continues until data saturation — no new themes emerging (often 10–15 in-depth interviews).
  • Data collection tools: semi-structured in-depth interviews, focus-group discussions, non-participant observation and document review.
  • Interviews are audio-recorded with consent and transcribed verbatim.
  • Analysis: thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke) — familiarisation → coding → themes → review → definition → report.
  • Content analysis is another option; the framework approach suits policy research.
  • Software (NVivo/ATLAS.ti) assists but does not replace the analyst.
  • Analysis proceeds at the same time as data collection.
  • Trustworthiness (Lincoln & Guba) — credibility (triangulation, member-checking).
  • Transferability (thick description).
  • Dependability (audit trail).
  • Confirmability (reflexivity).
  • These four are the qualitative counterparts of validity and reliability.
  • Reproduce the qualitative pipeline diagram with the constant-comparison loop and the four trustworthiness criteria.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 3b-vi and 3c-iv.
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research. 4th ed. (reference 11).
  • Braun V, Clarke V. Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qual Res Psychol. 2006;3:77–101. (primary method reference)
610 marks

Q6. Write note on fundamentals of Human energy transfer?

Full answer →

Cover the two laws of thermodynamics in the body, ATP as the energy currency, the three energy systems, and efficiency plus physiological application.

  • Marks plan: laws of thermodynamics as applied to the body (2), ATP — the energy currency and coupled reactions (2.5), the three energy systems (3), efficiency & physiological application (2.5).
  • Connect each energy system to a physiotherapy activity — the examiner wants the physiology applied, not just listed.
  • First law of thermodynamics (conservation): energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted.
  • The human machine converts the chemical energy of food into mechanical work, heat and stored energy.
  • Second law: conversions are inefficient; much energy is lost as heat — which is why exercising bodies warm up.
  • Biogenic molecules are reduced (energy-rich) and are oxidised to CO₂ and H₂O to release free energy.
  • ATP is the universal currency: cells cannot use food energy directly, so all transfers pass through ATP.
  • The terminal phosphate bond of ATP releases about 7.3 kcal/mol on hydrolysis.
  • ATP is regenerated by phosphorylation of ADP through coupled reactions.
  • Substrate-level phosphorylation happens in glycolysis and via creatine phosphate.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation happens in the mitochondrial electron-transport chain.
  • The CP shuttle is the fastest regeneration route: ADP + CP → ATP + creatine, catalysed by creatine kinase.
  • System 1 — ATP-PC (phosphagen): immediate, about 10 s of explosive power, anaerobic, no lactate.
  • System 2 — Anaerobic glycolysis: from 10 s to about 2 min of high-intensity effort; rapid ATP but limited by H⁺/lactate accumulation.
  • System 3 — Oxidative (aerobic) system: oxidises carbohydrate and fat; unlimited duration at lower intensity, dominant after about 2 min.
  • Fat yields more ATP per gram but needs more oxygen.
  • Whole-body mechanical efficiency is only about 20–25% (cycle ergometry); the rest becomes heat.
  • This heat is the physiological basis of warm-up, of thermoregulation during exercise, and of caloric-expenditure calculations.
  • Useful numbers: 1 L O₂ ≈ 5 kcal; MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min.
  • Training shifts substrate use (more fat oxidation at higher intensities in the trained) and raises the lactate threshold — the basis of every endurance prescription.
  • Reproduce the power–duration curve with the three energy systems fenced off along the time axis.
  • Physiotherapy links: phosphagen = a single hoist transfer in the gym; glycolytic = 2-min TUG repetitions; oxidative = a walking programme.
  • Fick's equation can cameo for the aerobic system.

Energy systems run 10 : 2 : ∞ — ATP–PC about 10 seconds, glycolysis about 2 minutes, oxidative forever.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 4a, 4g.
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance. 8th ed. Lippincott (syllabus Paper-I reference 13).
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier.
710 marks

Q7. Briefly prescribe the exercise protocol for weight control?

Full answer →

Write an actual FITT-based weight-control prescription: assessment and goals, energy deficit, aerobic FITT, resistance and behaviour, plus progression and precautions.

  • Marks plan: assessment & goal setting (1.5), energy balance & target deficit (2), aerobic FITT prescription (2.5), resistance + behavioural components (2), progression, precautions, Indian context (2).
  • "Prescribe" is the operative word — write an actual FITT table, not an essay on obesity.
  • An answer without frequency/intensity/time/type numbers is a 5/10 however beautifully written.
  • Assessment: baseline BMI + waist circumference.
  • Indian cutoffs: waist ≥90 cm in men / ≥80 cm in women = abdominal obesity.
  • Also assess body composition if available, use PAR-Q+ screening, check joint status (knees take the first brunt in the obese), resting BP and blood sugar.
  • Goal: 0.5–1 kg/week; a 5–10% weight loss over 3–6 months is already clinically meaningful.
  • Energy-balance principle: weight falls only in negative balance.
  • Target a deficit of 500–750 kcal/day (≈ 1200–1500 kcal diet for women / 1500–1800 for men) plus exercise.
  • Exercise alone contributes 200–400 kcal/session — diet and activity act together.
  • Aerobic prescription (the core of the answer): follow the FITT principle.
  • Frequency: 5–7 days/week.
  • Intensity: 60–75% HR reserve / RPE 11–14.
  • Time: 45–60 min continuous or accumulated in 10-min bouts.
  • Type: brisk walking, cycling, aqua-jogging — progress from 150 min/week to 250–300 min/week of moderate aerobic activity.
  • Obese or knee-compromised starters should use non-weight-bearing modes (cycling, swimming) initially.
  • Resistance training: progressive, 2–3 days/week, 8–10 large-muscle exercises, 2–3 sets of 10–15 at 60–70% 1RM.
  • Resistance preserves lean mass during dieting and raises resting metabolism.
  • Behavioural scaffolding: goal-setting, self-monitoring (build steps to 8,000–10,000/day), stimulus control, family involvement.
  • Progression: increase load and duration by about 5–10% every 2 weeks.
  • Precautions: watch for knee/back pain (modify mode), exercise-induced asthma, hypoglycaemia in diabetics on medication, and heat intolerance.
  • Maintenance: 200–300 min/week activity plus monthly weigh-ins — relapse prevention is the real challenge.
  • Reproduce the energy-balance seesaw diagram, then write the FITT table beside it.

Weight control numbers: deficit 500–750 kcal/day → 0.5–1 kg/week; goal 5–10% body weight in 3–6 months. FITT = Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 4f.
  • ACSM. Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription / Resource Manual (MSK syllabus reference 12).
  • McArdle, Katch & Katch. Exercise Physiology. 8th ed. (Paper-I reference 13).
  • Misra A et al. JAPI 2009 consensus (Indian cutoffs).
810 marks

Q8. Analyze the Instrumentation for neuromuscular electrical stimulation?

Full answer →

Draw and explain the NMES block diagram, give the waveform and key parameters with exact values, electrode technique, and precautions/uses.

  • Marks plan: block diagram & function of each component (3), waveform & key parameters (3), electrodes & application technique (2), precautions & clinical uses (2).
  • The examiner wants the physiology link: tie every parameter to a nerve-physiology fact (frequency→tetany; duration→motor fibre recruitment threshold).
  • "Charge-balanced biphasic prevents skin irritation" is a distinction line.
  • Block diagram chain: mains/power supply (battery → stabilised DC).
  • Oscillator/pulse generator: sets frequency and pulse duration via timing circuits.
  • Control/timer unit: sets the on-off cycle and ramp.
  • Amplifier: raises the signal to the required voltage/current.
  • Output/transformer + coupling: safety isolation and charge-balanced output.
  • Then electrodes → tissue.
  • Modern units are digital: microprocessor-generated pulsed currents with user-set parameters.
  • Waveform: symmetrical or asymmetrical biphasic pulsed current is preferred.
  • Biphasic is charge-balanced → no skin irritation under electrodes; monophasic pulsed (faradic-type) causes chemical polarisation.
  • Frequency (pulses/s): 30–50 pps for functional tetanic contraction (typical NMES 35–50 Hz).
  • Russian current: 2.5 kHz carrier modulated at 50 bursts/s for torque.
  • Low rates (2–10 Hz) are used for sensory/analgesic or muscle-pumping effects.
  • Pulse duration: 200–400 μs suits motor stimulation of large muscles (shorter for small muscles).
  • Amplitude (intensity): to strong but comfortable tetany, typically 20–100 mA depending on impedance.
  • Duty cycle / on:off: 1:3 to 1:5 (e.g. 10 s on, 30–50 s off) to postpone fatigue.
  • Stimulated muscle fatigues faster than voluntary contraction.
  • Ramp-up: 1–2 s for comfort.
  • Electrodes: place a large motor electrode over the muscle's motor point, and a smaller/dispersive electrode at the distal tendon or the opposite side of the belly.
  • Electrode size governs current density; use low-impedance hydrogel pads.
  • Skin preparation and exact motor-point mapping determine efficiency.
  • Precautions/contraindications: avoid pacemakers/implanted devices, pregnancy over the uterus, active malignancy in the region, thrombosis, and broken skin.
  • Uses: muscle strengthening/re-education after injury or surgery (e.g. post-TKR quadriceps), disuse atrophy, NMES-assisted gait, oedema pumping, and preserving muscle plasticity.
  • Reproduce the NMES block diagram: five boxes, each labelled with the parameter it controls.

Russian current: 2.5 kHz carrier, 50 bursts/s, 10:50 on:off. Motor NMES: 35–50 Hz, 200–400 µs, duty cycle 1:3–1:5.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 5 (a–e).
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. — membrane/action potential chapters.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — electrical muscle stimulation sections.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (MSK syllabus reference 10).
910 marks

Q9. Psychometric Properties of SPADI

Full answer →

Give the structure and scoring of SPADI, then its reliability, validity, responsiveness and MCID, with the exact values and clinical interpretation.

  • Marks plan: structure & scoring of SPADI (3), reliability (2.5), validity (2), responsiveness & MCID (1.5), clinical interpretation & versions (1).
  • Psychometric properties = reliability + validity + responsiveness. An answer that gives only structure caps at 5/10.
  • Quote ICC, alpha and MCID values with their meaning in one bracket each — exact decimals to one place are enough, and never invent a value you don't remember.
  • The instrument: SPADI (Shoulder Pain and Disability Index, Roach et al. 1991) is a 13-item self-report, region-specific measure for shoulder pathology.
  • It has 5 pain items: pain at its worst, lying on the involved side, reaching up high, touching the back of the neck, and pushing with the involved arm.
  • It has 8 disability items covering daily self-care and lifting tasks — washing hair, washing the back, dressing, fastening behind the back, carrying heavy objects and similar.
  • Each item sits on a 0–10 NRS/VAS.
  • Scores are averaged and expressed as a percentage (0–100) — higher = worse.
  • Reliability: test–retest ICC 0.84–0.94 across studies over 1–2 weeks in stable patients.
  • Internal consistency: Cronbach's α 0.86–0.98 for subscales and total.
  • A Cronbach's alpha >0.9 here shows the items measure one construct — with a caution against item redundancy.
  • Validity — content/face: developed from patients' own reports (37 patients in the original development study; later validation studies enlarged the base).
  • Validity — construct: convergent correlations with the DASH (r ≈ 0.6–0.8), goniometric ROM and pain ratings.
  • Validity — cross-cultural: validated translations (Hindi, Kannada, Marathi, Tamil, Chinese, Portuguese, etc.) with equivalent factor structure.
  • Responsiveness: effect sizes 0.8–1.4 across interventions (frozen shoulder, RC pathology).
  • MCID ≈ 8–10 points (7–13% in various studies) — below that, change is measurement noise.
  • No floor/ceiling problems in typical MSK shoulder populations, unlike generic measures.
  • Interpretation: use it for tracking individual progress and as a research endpoint.
  • Pair it with objective measures (ROM, strength) for a complete ICF picture — SPADI maps largely to activity/participation, not body structure.
  • Reproduce the SPADI splitting-box diagram: 13 items → 5 pain + 8 disability → 0–100%.

SPADI = 5 + 8 = 13 items, 0–100, higher = worse; MCID ≈ 8–10, MDC95 ≈ 18. QuickDASH cuts it to 11 items.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 1 (standardized scales & psychometric properties).
  • Roach KE, Budiman-Mak E, Songsiridej N, Lertratanakul Y. Development of a shoulder pain and disability index. Arthritis Care Res. 1991;4:143–9. (primary)
  • Williams JW et al. Responsive and important: SPADI vs SF-36. J Clin Epidemiol. (responsiveness evidence)
  • Hicks CM. Research Methods for Clinical Therapists. (psychometric interpretation — Indian MPT standard)
1010 marks

Q10. What is formulated intended learning outcomes? Explain in detail the six objectives of Bloom's Taxonomy?

Full answer →

Define an intended learning outcome (SMART, with structure), then explain the six levels of Bloom's revised taxonomy with a physiotherapy example each, plus constructive alignment.

  • Marks plan: definition & qualities (SMART) of an ILO (1.5), structure of an ILO statement (1.5), six levels of Bloom's (revised) taxonomy with examples (5), application in physiotherapy teaching + conclusion (2).
  • Two credit-earning moves: write one complete model ILO, and say "constructive alignment" with Bloom + Miller in the conclusion.
  • An ILO is a statement, written before teaching begins, of what the learner is expected to know, do or value at the end of a defined learning episode.
  • It is the destination the teacher designs towards (Tyler's rationale: objectives → experiences → organisation → evaluation).
  • Good ILOs are SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
  • Use observable action verbs ("demonstrate", "differentiate") rather than vague ones ("understand", "know").
  • Structure: "By the end of this session, the student will be able to <action verb> <content> <context/standard>."
  • Bloom's original 1956 taxonomy (knowledge → evaluation) was revised by Anderson & Krathwohl (2001) into verb-form levels.
  • Level 1 — Remember: recall facts, e.g. list the six determinants of gait.
  • Level 2 — Understand: explain concepts, e.g. explain the gate-control theory in your own words.
  • Level 3 — Apply: use in new situations, e.g. apply the Fick equation to an exercise prescription.
  • Level 4 — Analyse: decompose relationships, e.g. differentiate neuropathic from nociceptive pain patterns in a case.
  • Level 5 — Evaluate: judge with criteria, e.g. appraise an RCT's methodological quality and decide whether to apply its result.
  • Level 6 — Create: produce new work, e.g. design a 6-week rehabilitation protocol for a post-TKR patient.
  • Write a physiotherapy example next to each level — evaluators check for the examples, not just the ladder.
  • Why it matters: ILOs align teaching, assessment and content — this is constructive alignment (Biggs).
  • Example of misalignment: a viva that only asks "define…" while the ILO promised "design a protocol".
  • Miller's pyramid (knows → knows how → shows → does) shapes competency-based education.
  • Bloom's lower levels map onto "knows/knows how", while clinical demonstration maps to "shows/does".
  • Model ILO to reproduce: "By the end of this session, the student will be able to demonstrate the modified Ober's test on a peer without prompting."
  • Reproduce Bloom's pyramid (revised) with a physiotherapy example beside each level.

Bloom's verbs climb R-U-A-A-E-C: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. Miller's pyramid peaks at Does.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 6 (a–c).
  • Anderson LW, Krathwohl DR (eds). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing. 2001 (revision of Bloom 1956).
  • Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Acad Med. 1990 (Miller's pyramid).
  • Biggs J. Teaching for Quality Learning at University. (constructive alignment)
110 marks

What are the articulating structures in the musculoskeletal system? Explain in detail about them.

Full answer →

Explain the four tissue families that make and move a joint, then classify joints properly with examples.

  • What earns marks: introduce the MSK system and its articulating components (1 mark) · cover bone, cartilage, joint classification and the synovial joint structure — each is a separate mark block · draw and label a typical synovial joint — this earns the diagram mark · keep the pyramid visible — fibrous, then cartilaginous, then synovial, then the six synovial types with examples.
  • The musculoskeletal system is made of joints between bones, held together by connective tissue, and moved by the neuro-muscular unit.
  • A joint (articulation) is the site where two or more bones meet, whether or not movement happens there.
  • Four families of structures take part in a joint: bone, cartilage, the fibrous capsule–ligament complex, and the muscle–tendon unit — all supervised by the nervous system.
  • Bone: the adult skeleton has 206 bones — 80 axial and 126 appendicular.
  • Bone types: long, short, flat, irregular and sesamoid.
  • A long bone has an epiphysis (covered by hyaline articular cartilage) at each end, a metaphysis, and a diaphysis of dense cortical bone enclosing the medullary cavity.
  • Functions of bone: protection, mineral store (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻), blood cell formation (haemopoiesis), muscle attachment, and carrying compressive forces. Wolff's law: bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress.
  • Bone composition: about 35% organic matrix (mainly type I collagen, osteoid) giving tensile strength, and about 65% inorganic hydroxyapatite giving compressive rigidity.
  • Bone has blood vessels and periosteal nerves, so fracture pain is sharp and localised — unlike cartilage, which has no nerves and no blood supply.
  • Hyaline (articular) cartilage: covers the weight-bearing ends of bones in synovial joints; type II collagen; avascular, aneural and alymphatic; fed by synovial fluid diffusion and cyclic loading. Low friction (coefficient ~0.01) and load distribution.
  • Fibrocartilage: dense type I collagen; forms labra (glenoid, acetabular), knee menisci, intervertebral discs and articular discs (TMJ); resists compression and shear.
  • Elastic cartilage: contains elastin; found in the ear and epiglottis.
  • Joint classification (1) Fibrous joints — bones united by fibrous tissue, minimal movement: sutures of the skull (synarthrosis), syndesmosis (inferior tibiofibular joint, interosseous membranes), and gomphosis (tooth in socket).
  • Joint classification (2) Cartilaginous joints — united by cartilage: synchondrosis (epiphyseal/growth plate, first costochondral — temporary, hyaline) and symphysis (pubic symphysis, intervertebral disc — permanent, fibrocartilage, slight movement).
  • Joint classification (3) Synovial (diarthrodial) joints — freely movable, the most important group clinically.
  • Synovial types by shape and axes: Plane/gliding (acromioclavicular, intercarpal — non-axial); Hinge (elbow ulnohumeral, ankle, IP joints — uniaxial); Pivot (atlanto-axial, superior radio-ulnar — uniaxial rotation); Condyloid/ellipsoid (MCP, wrist — biaxial); Saddle (first CMC thumb, sternoclavicular — biaxial); Ball-and-socket (shoulder glenohumeral, hip — multiaxial).
  • Structure of a typical synovial joint — articular (hyaline) cartilage: a 2–4 mm thick bearing surface.
  • Joint capsule: an outer fibrous capsule (dense irregular connective tissue) plus an inner synovial membrane that secretes synovial fluid (~1–3 mL in a knee), a dialysate of plasma plus hyaluronic acid; it lubricates and nourishes cartilage.
  • Ligaments: intrinsic thickenings of the capsule (e.g. glenohumeral ligaments) and extrinsic check-reins (e.g. coracohumeral); mainly type I collagen, with mechanoreceptors at insertions — the basis of reflex joint stabilisation.
  • Accessory structures: intra-articular fibrocartilaginous discs/menisci, labra that deepen sockets, bursae, and fat pads (Hoffa's) filling dead space.

Joint classification anchor: what tissue unites the bones? Fibrous (suture, syndesmosis) — cartilaginous (synchondrosis = hyaline, symphysis = disc) — synovial (cavity + cartilage + capsule). The intervertebral disc is a symphysis.

How do you calculate BMI? Mention its application in degenerative conditions.

Full answer →

Show the BMI formula with a real worked example, give WHO and Asian-Indian cut-offs, then link BMI to degenerative joint and disc problems.

  • What earns marks: define BMI and place it in anthropometry (1.5 marks) · write the formula and do a real worked example with units (2 marks) · give both the WHO table and the Asian-Indian cut-offs (2.5 marks) · apply BMI to degenerative conditions — OA, disc, sarcopenia (3 marks) · finish with the limitations of BMI and a conclusion (1 mark).
  • BMI (Body Mass Index, formerly Quetelet's index) is an anthropometric index of weight-for-height used to sort people into body-size categories.
  • Formula: BMI = weight (kg) / height² (m²).
  • Worked example: a 58-year-old woman weighing 68 kg with height 1.55 m → BMI = 68 / (1.55 × 1.55) = 68 / 2.40 = 28.3 kg/m² → Class I obesity by Indian criteria.
  • Measurement technique: wall-mounted stadiometer, shoes off, weight on a calibrated balance in minimal clothing.
  • WHO classification: 18.5–24.9 normal; 25–29.9 overweight; 30–34.9 obese class I; 35–39.9 obese class II; ≥ 40 obese class III.
  • Asian-Indian consensus: 18.0–22.9 normal; 23–24.9 overweight; ≥ 25 obese.
  • Indians develop metabolic risk at a lower BMI (the 'thin-fat Indian phenotype'), so Indian cut-offs are stricter than WHO global cut-offs.
  • Application — joint load: each step transmits about 3–4 times body weight through the knee; every extra kilogram of fat multiplies tibiofemoral and patellofemoral load over thousands of steps per day → accelerated cartilage wear in knee osteoarthritis.
  • Obesity is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for knee OA, particularly in women.
  • Application — inflammation: adipose tissue is metabolically active; an imbalance of adipokines (leptin, adiponectin) acts as a systemic inflammatory drive that worsens synovitis and pain in OA and chronic low-back degeneration.
  • Application — prognosis and triage: BMI decides whether arthroplasty risk counselling (wound healing, infection, anaesthetic risk) is needed, and guides conservative versus surgical planning.
  • Application — physiotherapy prescription: high BMI changes exercise selection — non/low-weight-bearing aerobic work (cycling, aqua therapy) early, treadmill jogging later; it also re-baselines the MET targets for endurance dosing.
  • Application — outcome prediction: weight reduction of ~10% with exercise gives clinically meaningful functional improvement and pain relief in overweight/obese knee-OA patients (IDEA trial evidence).
  • Application — low BMI in the elderly: flags sarcopenia and fall/fracture risk, poor bone stock (osteoporosis screening) and poor postural endurance — degeneration is not only an overweight story.
  • Limitations: BMI cannot tell fat mass from lean mass (a stocky athlete reads as 'obese'), says nothing about fat distribution (add waist circumference / waist-hip ratio), and is unreliable in pregnancy, oedema and amputees.
  • Conclusion: used together with waist circumference and body-composition methods, BMI remains the fastest screening anthropometric tool in an Indian outpatient department.

Asian-Indian cut-offs: BMI 23 overweight, 25 obese; waist ≥90 cm (men) / ≥80 cm (women) = abdominal obesity.

Sources

310 marks

Role of power and endurance in training.

Full answer →

Define strength, power and endurance precisely, explain their physiology, and show how power and endurance are trained and used in rehab.

  • What earns marks: define strength, power and endurance with units and formula (2.5 marks) · explain the physiological basis — fibre types and energy systems (2 marks) · give the role of power in training and the role of endurance in training, each with a clinical application (2 + 2 marks) · close with the interplay of the three and the training principles (1.5 marks).
  • Strength: the ability of a muscle or muscle group to generate force against a resistance.
  • Power: the rate of doing work — Power = Work / Time = Force × Velocity (measured in watts). It has both a force component and a speed component.
  • Endurance: the ability to sustain a physical activity (whole-body), or to perform repeated muscle contractions (muscle endurance) against a submaximal resistance for an extended time.
  • Force–velocity curve (Hill): as contraction speed rises, force falls; power peaks at about one-third of maximum shortening velocity (roughly the 30–50% 1RM region).
  • Muscle fibre types: type I (slow oxidative — fatigue-resistant, mitochondria-rich → endurance machinery); type IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic — the hybrid, both force and endurance); type IIx (fast glycolytic — force and power, fatigable).
  • Energy supply follows the task: ATP-PC (phosphagen) for seconds of explosive power, anaerobic glycolysis for ~2 minutes of high effort, and the oxidative (aerobic) system — the only sustainable one — for endurance.
  • Motor-unit recruitment follows the size principle: small units first, large high-force units only when demand is high.
  • Role of power: real-life function is a power demand — rising from a chair, stair ascent, a cricketer's bowling action, a sprinter's push-off.
  • Loss of power (sarcopenia hits fast fibres hardest) explains why elderly patients fall during quick corrections of balance.
  • Power training method: moderate loads moved as fast as possible (30–60% 1RM for upper body, 0–60% for lower-body ballistic work, ACSM), and plyometrics — stretch-shortening cycle drills (box jumps, medicine-ball throws).
  • Power adaptations: improved rate of force development, motor-unit firing frequency and synchronisation, elastic-tendon stiffness, and inter-muscular coordination — largely neural.
  • Power in MSK rehab: late-stage ACL/arthroplasty return-to-sport criteria include hop tests — pure strength clearance is not enough; power plus landing mechanics decide safe return.
  • Role of endurance: endurance is the platform for recovery and repeated function — the postural muscles (trunk stabilisers, soleus) are endurance organs by design.
  • Endurance training method: low load, high repetitions (muscle endurance: > 12–15 reps); at VO₂max it decreases resting heart rate and improves autonomic balance.
  • Endurance in clinic: endurance work counters fatigue-related compensations — e.g. the tired knee-OA patient who develops a vaulting gait at 200 m; scapular-stabiliser endurance prevents late rotator-cuff overload.
  • Interplay: strength, power and endurance lie on one continuum of muscle performance, and both power and endurance come from a strength base — power = strength expressed fast, endurance = strength sustained.
  • Prescription follows the SAID principle (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand) and overload; sequence strength → power → endurance within a periodised plan.
Sources

410 marks

Describe about the oxygen supply during training in post-traumatic knee stiffness.

Full answer →

Trace oxygen from air to muscle using the Fick equation, then apply it to what goes wrong in a stiff knee after trauma.

  • What earns marks: draw the oxygen transport chain — ventilation → diffusion → circulation → extraction (3 marks) · write the Fick principle and the exercise response (HR, SV, CO, a-vO₂ diff) (2 marks) · explain local muscle adaptations — capillary bed, arterioles, muscle pump (2 marks) · link trauma and immobilisation to lost oxidative capacity in the stiff knee (2 marks) — keep saying 'post-traumatic knee stiffness' · end with training implications (1 mark).
  • The oxygen transport chain has four linked steps: pulmonary ventilation, diffusion, circulatory transport, and peripheral extraction.
  • Pulmonary ventilation: alveolar ventilation rises from ~6 L/min at rest to ~100+ L/min in maximal exercise (both respiratory rate and tidal volume climb).
  • Diffusion across the alveolo-capillary membrane: driven by a PO₂ gradient of about 60 mmHg — alveolar PO₂ ~104 mmHg versus venous PO₂ ~40 mmHg at rest, widening during exercise as venous PO₂ falls.
  • Circulatory transport: cardiac output rises from ~5 L/min to ~20–25 L/min in young adults; the Frank–Starling mechanism (increased venous return stretches the ventricle) plus sympathetic drive raise both stroke volume and heart rate.
  • Peripheral extraction: the arterio-venous O₂ difference widens (from ~4–5 to ~15+ mL O₂/dL) as working muscle pulls oxygen out of blood.
  • Fick equation: VO₂ = Cardiac Output × a-vO₂ difference — every training adaptation fits into one of its two terms.
  • Local supply — arteriolar dilatation: local metabolites (CO₂, H⁺/lactate, adenosine, K⁺) relax arteriolar smooth muscle; muscle blood flow rises up to 15–20-fold (far beyond the ~4–5-fold rise in cardiac output) because flow is also redistributed from splanchnic and non-working beds.
  • Local supply — capillary recruitment: at rest some capillaries are closed; exercise opens the reserve, shortening diffusion distance.
  • Local supply — the muscle pump: rhythmic contraction milks venous blood proximally and venous valves keep it one-way; this is why pain-free, active cyclical exercise beats passive work for stiff knees.
  • Local supply — oxygen extraction: myoglobin releases O₂ as PO₂ falls, and the Bohr effect (acidosis shifts the Hb-dissociation curve right) unloads more O₂ exactly where it is needed.
  • In post-traumatic knee stiffness (after intra-/peri-articular fracture, multi-ligament injury or prolonged immobilisation): disuse atrophy hits the quadriceps, preferentially the type I (slow oxidative) fibres of vastus medialis obliquus and the anti-gravity extensors; mitochondrial density and oxidative enzyme activity fall → early fatigability.
  • Capillarisation is reduced and re-perfusion after ischaemic effort is prolonged; effusion and capsular tightening raise intra-compartmental pressure and can further impede perfusion at low angles of knee flexion.
  • Pain inhibition (arthrogenous muscle inhibition) delays activation — recruitment of large motor units suffers, so the patient fatigues long before the target repetition range.
  • Training implication: start early with pain-free cyclical, rhythmic activity (stationary cycling with the seat raised, foot pumps, heel slides) to use the muscle pump without provoking reactive synovitis.
  • Isometrics in a pain-free arc sustain trophic tone — but sustained maximal isometrics occlude local blood flow; use rhythmic/brief-hold isometrics (hold 6 s, breathe, repeat ×10) so oxygen delivery continues between holds.
  • Avoid the Valsalva manoeuvre — breath-holding against a closed glottis spikes blood pressure and reduces venous return; teach exhale-on-effort.
  • Progress toward aerobic conditioning (walk/cycle programmes at ~60% HR reserve) to rebuild the central oxygen-transport capacity that bed-rest deconditioning erodes; add interval work only after reactive inflammation settles.
  • Warm-up literally raises tissue temperature and shifts the Hb curve rightward — a physiologic justification every answer should include.

Write Fick and annotate: VO₂ = (HR × SV) × (a−v)O₂ — each term is one adaptation site of aerobic training.

  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. F.A. Davis — aerobic endurance and isometric exercise sections.
510 marks

Applied mechanics and pathomechanics following rotator cuff injury.

Full answer →

Give the normal shoulder mechanics first (force couple, concavity compression, scapulohumeral rhythm), then show how a cuff tear breaks them.

  • What earns marks: applied anatomy of the cuff (SITS) and the glenohumeral stability problem (2 marks) · normal applied mechanics — concavity compression, force couple, scapulohumeral rhythm (3 marks) · pathomechanics after a cuff tear — head migration, impingement, rhythm breakdown (3.5 marks) · functional consequences plus a labelled diagram (1.5 marks).
  • The glenohumeral (GH) joint trades bony congruence for range of motion: the large humeral head sits on a small, shallow glenoid cavity (only about a third of the head is in contact at any position), deepened a little by the glenoid labrum.
  • Static restraints (capsule, glenohumeral ligaments) are lax by design, so dynamic stability depends on the rotator cuff — supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis (SITS).
  • Concavity compression: supraspinatus, and the cuff as a whole, compresses the humeral head into the concave glenoid — the primary mechanism keeping the head centred through mid-range, where the ligaments are slack.
  • Transverse (force) couple: during abduction the deltoid's line of pull passes above the centre of the head and would translate it upward; the inferiorly-directed pull of subscapularis (anterior) and infraspinatus + teres minor (posterior) depresses and centres the head. Cuff–deltoid balance converts deltoid's shear into pure rotation.
  • Scapulohumeral rhythm: a ~2:1 ratio — for 180° of elevation, ~120° occurs at GH and ~60° at scapulothoracic (upward rotation by trapezius/serratus anterior), keeping the glenoid track facing the moving head and preserving the subacromial space.
  • Supraspinatus also contributes an initial abduction torque and, with the others, provides proprioceptive guarding — the reflex stiffening of the joint under load.
  • After a cuff tear — loss of concavity compression and depressor action → superior translation of the humeral head during elevation: the deltoid now pulls the head upward unopposed against the coraco-acromial arch.
  • Secondary subacromial impingement: the head, greater tuberosity and bursal tissue crowd the subacromial space, already narrowed in abduction–external rotation positions; repetitive micro-trauma → bursitis, tendinopathy, partial- then full-thickness tear (a self-perpetuating cycle).
  • Scapulohumeral rhythm breakdown: pain inhibits serratus anterior/lower trapezius, producing scapular dyskinesis (excessive scapular elevation, reduced upward rotation, dysrhythmia); the glenoid no longer follows the head, so GH elevation reduces and scapular substitution (shoulder shrug) appears.
  • Strength and function: painful arc and weak abduction/external rotation; night pain lying on the side is classical. In massive chronic tears the head may erode the acromion — cuff-tear arthropathy.
  • Glenohumeral arthrokinematics change: the normal spin of the head is replaced by an abnormal roll-and-slide, further jamming the head under the arch.
  • Clinical consequence: the patient loses smooth overhead function and, untreated, enters the impingement–tear–weakness cycle; rehabilitation therefore restores the depressor/cuff–deltoid force couple and scapular control before loading power.

SITS = Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis. The cuff is the deltoid's brake — depressor force couple keeping the head centred in the glenoid.

Define Posture. Explain the methods to control posture following IVDP.

Full answer →

Define posture, describe normal postural control, explain what IVDP changes, then give the methods to control posture after IVDP.

  • What earns marks: define posture (classic + physiological) (1.5 marks) · describe the normal postural control mechanism — sensory inputs, integration, outputs (2.5 marks) · explain what IVDP changes — direction-specific disc mechanics (2 marks) · give the methods to control posture after IVDP — the core of the answer (3.5 marks) · end with a conclusion (0.5 mark). Write 'intervertebral disc prolapse' in full once.
  • Posture is the relative alignment of body segments to one another and to gravity at any given moment — classically, 'the position from which movement begins and ends.'
  • Ideal upright posture: the plumb line passes through the ear, shoulder, hip, knee and lateral malleolus, with the cervical and lumbar lordoses balanced by the thoracic and sacral kyphoses.
  • Sensory input: visual (eyes), vestibular (otoliths for static, semi-circular canals for dynamic), and somatosensory/proprioceptive input from joints, muscles and skin — the dominant input in healthy adults.
  • Central integration: spinal reflex arcs (stretch reflex for tone), brainstem (vestibulo- and rectospinal tracts), cerebellum (timing/smoothing), and cortical representation for anticipatory and voluntary corrections.
  • Motor output: tonic postural muscles and phasic mobilisers, plus anticipatory feed-forward postural adjustments (transversus abdominis fires before limb movement) and reactive strategies — ankle, hip and stepping strategies.
  • In intervertebral disc prolapse (IVDP), a posterior/postero-lateral prolapse (the common direction) is aggravated by flexion + loading, which raises intradiscal pressure and pushes nuclear material backward toward the posterior annulus and nerve root — the basis of a peripheralising pain pattern.
  • Patients adopt a shift/list, lose the lumbar lordosis and reflexively inhibit their deep stabilisers (transversus abdominis, multifidus) through pain.
  • The goal of postural control after IVDP is to maintain the neutral spine — the position of least disc stress — and to abolish peripheralisation (McKenzie's centralisation principle).
  • Method — education and conscious correction: teach neutral spine in sitting, standing and lifting; avoid prolonged flexion and avoid combining flexion with rotation (the classic provocative couple); use a lumbar roll/cushion for chair sitting with knees and hips at 90° and feet supported; a reclined posture lowers disc load — Nachemson's classic intradiscal-pressure studies showed slumped sitting loads the L3–4 disc more than standing.
  • Method — positioning and bed-rest discipline: short-term rest in the most reducing posture (commonly prone extension or side-lying with a pillow between the knees); use the log-rolling technique to get in and out of bed; avoid early-morning unsupported sitting (the disc is hydrated and turgid after overnight water imbibition).
  • Method — core stabilisation programme: re-train transversus abdominis drawing-in, multifidus activation, diaphragmatic breathing and pelvic floor co-activation — progressing from isolated activation to integrated functional positions (hook-lying → quadruped → standing).
  • Method — direction-specific exercise (McKenzie method): prone/supported extension to centralise symptoms when the derangement responds to extension; the sagittal-plane rule — movements that centralise pain are prescribed, those that peripheralise are avoided.
  • Method — proprioceptive/balance retraining: wobble-board and unstable-surface work to restore somatosensory postural reflexes once pain settles.
  • Method — ergonomics and ADL modification: workstation redesign, hip-hinge lifting with the load close to the body, micro-breaks every 30–40 min, and avoidance of prolonged flexion postures.
  • Method — external support: a temporary lumbosacral corset as a proprioceptive reminder — never a substitute for the muscle corset.
  • Method — general conditioning: weight reduction, a walking programme and thoracic mobility work to distribute stress across the whole spine.

Posture control pair: TrA = corset, multifidus = segmental strings; feed-forward fires BEFORE the limb moves — delayed after LBP.

710 marks

Define Gait. Describe the determinants of gait with examples.

Full answer →

Define gait and the gait cycle, explain why the determinants exist, then give all six determinants with their values and examples.

  • What earns marks: define gait and the gait cycle in brief — stance/swing, 60:40 (1.5 marks) · explain the problem the determinants solve — the centre-of-mass trajectory without them (1.5 marks) · give all six determinants, each with mechanism + value + example (6 marks). The values (4°, 4–5°, 15–18°, ~2.5 cm) are what earn first-class marks · close on energy conservation and add a diagram (1 mark).
  • Gait is the manner or style of walking — the pattern of locomotion produced by the cyclic, coordinated movement of body segments.
  • One gait cycle = heel strike of one foot to the next heel strike of the same foot: a stance phase (60%) and a swing phase (40%).
  • The two phases together span eight phases of the cycle: IC → LR → MSt → TSt → PSw | ISw → MSw → TSw.
  • Why determinants exist: if the legs were rigid struts and the pelvis fixed, the body's centre of mass (COM) would travel in a series of arcs as high as each leg-length step-over, wasting enormous energy lifting and dropping the body ~7–8 cm twice each step.
  • The six determinants of gait (Saunders, Inman & Eberhart) are the pelvic and lower-limb movements that flatten these arcs — cutting vertical COM displacement to about 5 cm (2 inch) and horizontal sway to ~2.5 cm, conserving energy.
  • Determinant 1 — Pelvic rotation: the pelvis rotates ~4° forward on the swing side (total ~8°) in the transverse plane at initial contact; this lengthens the step and flattens the arc's base. Example: loss of rotation after hip fusion forces the patient to 'square-off' and circumduct — a stiff, costlier gait.
  • Determinant 2 — Pelvic tilt (obliquity): the pelvis drops ~4–5° on the swing side (controlled eccentrically by the stance-side hip abductors — gluteus medius), lowering the apex of the COM arc. Example: abductor weakness (safe-side Trendelenburg pattern) produces an exaggerated drop and lateral lurch.
  • Determinant 3 — Knee flexion in stance: after loading response the knee stays flexed ~15–18° until mid-stance, shortening the stance limb exactly when the COM would otherwise be highest. Example: after knee fusion/arthrodesis the leg becomes a long lever and the patient vaults on the sound side to clear it.
  • Determinant 4 — Foot and ankle mechanisms: from heel strike (ankle plantarflexed with the heel as rocker) to foot-flat, then the ankle rocker, then heel-off with the forefoot rocker — a smooth rolling radius instead of a point pivot. Example: ankle equinus/calcaneus deformity after trauma destroys the rockers and substitutes hip circumduction.
  • Determinant 5 — Knee mechanisms: the knee's linked flexion with the ankle rockers at the start and end of stance; since the ankle plantarflexes while the knee flexes (and vice versa), the combined limb length stays nearly constant, again smoothing the COM path. Example: a stiff-knee gait (rectus femoris spasticity/post-op arthrofibrosis) produces compensatory hip-hiking in swing.
  • Determinant 6 — Lateral pelvic displacement: the pelvis (and COM) shifts ~2.5 cm over the weight-bearing limb in the frontal plane, with a functional genu valgum at the knee keeping the COM near the supporting foot. Example: coxa vara or a wide-based gait increases sway and the energy cost of walking.
  • Conclusion: the six determinants act as an energy-saving system — each flattens part of the COM trajectory, and the pathological gait deviations we treat (Trendelenburg lurch, circumduction, vaulting, hip hiking) are simply the loss of one or more determinants.
  • Quantify them clinically with observational video/10-metre walk analysis; the underlying principle is minimisation of energy expenditure.

Gait: stance 60 : swing 40; phases IC → LR → MSt → TSt → PSw | ISw → MSw → TSw; the six determinants exist to flatten the COM curve.

Explain the various theories of pain in detail.

Full answer →

Give the IASP definition and pathway, then work through specificity, intensity, pattern, gate control (in full) and neuromatrix — linking each to physiotherapy.

  • What earns marks: IASP definition + brief pain pathway (nociceptor → dorsal horn → spinothalamic) (2 marks) · specificity theory and intensity theory (1.5 marks) · pattern theory (1.5 marks) · gate control theory in full detail (Melzack & Wall) (3 marks) · neuromatrix theory + biopsychosocial conclusion + diagram (2 marks). Link each theory to one physiotherapy intervention.
  • IASP definition: pain is 'an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage.'
  • The pain pathway in one line: nociceptors → Aδ and C fibres → dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa) → decussation → lateral spinothalamic tract → thalamus → somatosensory cortex & limbic centres.
  • Specificity theory (von Frey, 1895): dedicated, hard-wired pain pathways exist — specialised nociceptors connect via dedicated fibres to a pain centre in the brain, just as vision has its own line.
  • Specificity — strengths: correct about specialised receptors and labelled lines (Aδ sharp/first pain, C dull/second pain). Fails to explain: phantom limb pain, chronic pain without ongoing tissue damage, and pain modulation by emotion/attention.
  • Intensity theory: an old proposal that pain is merely excessive stimulation of any sensory receptor — strong touch = pain. Largely of historical value; disproved because intense stimuli of a non-nociceptive kind do not reliably produce pain.
  • Pattern theory (Goldscheider, 1890s; revived by Weddell and Sinclair in the 1950s): pain is not a special sense but a pattern of neural firing — intense, frequent, temporally-patterned discharge from any receptor is decoded centrally as pain.
  • Pattern theory introduced the crucial idea of central processing and temporal summation (the ancestor of wind-up and central sensitisation), but underplayed the specificity of nociceptors.
  • Gate control theory (Melzack & Wall, 1965): a 'gate' in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa, lamina II) regulates transmission from peripheral afferents to transmission (T) cells that project up the spinothalamic tract.
  • Gate control — large-diameter Aβ (touch/mechanoreceptor) fibres excite the T cells but ALSO excite the substantia gelatinosa (SG) interneurons, which inhibit transmission → gate closes.
  • Gate control — small-diameter Aδ/C (nociceptive) fibres excite T cells and inhibit the SG interneurons → gate opens → pain ascends.
  • Gate control — central control: descending fibres from the brain (periaqueductal grey, raphe magnus — serotonergic/noradrenergic) can bias the gate — the physiology behind attention, anxiety, expectation and placebo changing pain.
  • Gate control clinical applications: TENS (large-fibre stimulation closing the gate), rubbing a knock, and cognitive reassurance reducing descending facilitation.
  • Gate control limitation: pain is more than a spinal gate — it does not account for chronic plasticity or emotional colour, which the next theory supplies.
  • Neuromatrix theory (Melzack, 1999): phantom limb pain in people without peripheral input forced the next leap — the brain contains a body-self neuromatrix, a widespread network (somatosensory, limbic, thalamic, parietal) that continuously generates the experience of the body.
  • Neuromatrix: pain is the output of this matrix, shaped by sensory, cognitive-evaluative and emotional-motivational dimensions — the neuroscientific scaffold of the biopsychosocial model used for chronic MSK pain, and the justification for pain neuroscience education, graded activity and cognitive-behavioural methods.
  • Conclusion: each theory is partly right — specificity gave us nociceptors, pattern gave us central processing, gate control gave us modulation (and TENS), and the neuromatrix gives us the modern biopsychosocial treatment of persistent pain.

Pain fibres: Aδ = fast & sharp (first pain), C = slow & dull (second pain). Gate theory: large-fibre input closes the gate on small-fibre traffic.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II Unit 9 — Pain: (a) definition, pathways, physiology/pathophysiology, (d) theories and models of pain; Paper IV Unit 2c/4d — educational, behavioural and cognitive methods in pain.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier — somatic sensations: pain, its pathways and the pain-suppression (descending) systems.
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965;150(3699):971–9. (primary source, cited for examiner-level completeness)
  • Melzack R. From the gate to the neuromatrix. Pain 1999;Suppl 6:S121–6.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. F.A. Davis — pain assessment and management chapters (syllabus reference 10).
910 marks

Write the biophysical effects of heat on various systems in the body.

Full answer →

Write the physics of heat transfer briefly, then the biophysical effects system by system, and finish with applications and precautions.

  • What earns marks: physics of heat transfer (conduction, convection, radiation, conversion) + superficial vs deep (2 marks) · local thermal response — metabolism, blood flow, capillary permeability (2.5 marks) · systemic effects — cardiovascular, neuromuscular, skin (3 marks) · therapeutic applications, precautions/contraindications + diagram (2.5 marks). Use headings: skin / cardiovascular / neuromuscular / connective tissue / joint.
  • Heat reaches tissue by four modes: conduction (hot packs, paraffin wax — direct contact), convection (hydrotherapy, fluidotherapy — moving medium), radiation (infrared lamp), and conversion (ultrasound, shortwave diathermy, microwave — energy converted to heat within tissue).
  • Superficial agents heat skin and subcutaneous tissue to ~1 cm; deep heating (ultrasound, SWD) reaches muscle-joint depths.
  • Local tissue temperature is the product of energy delivered, tissue depth and perfusion — the physiotherapist's dose, not the machine's dial, decides it.
  • Metabolic effect: tissue metabolism rises roughly 10–13% per 1 °C increase (van 't Hoff/Arrhenius-type Q₁₀ effect) — the basic biophysical justification of every heating agent. Heat in the inflammatory proliferative phase (after ~48 h) supports repair by raising metabolic and enzymatic activity.
  • Skin and subcutaneous tissue: cutaneous vasodilatation (heat-sensitive cutaneous receptors → sympathetic vasoconstrictor withdrawal), erythema, sweating, increased capillary permeability (mild oedema risk if overdone), and softening of scar/collagen.
  • Cardiovascular system: local vasodilatation increases blood flow (up to several-fold) with its fresh oxygen, leukocytes and nutrients — accelerating removal of pain metabolites (bradykinin, substance P).
  • Cardiovascular system (generalised heating): heart rate and cardiac output rise, peripheral resistance falls, and blood pressure may drop — hence cardiac patients need caution with large-area heating.
  • Neuromuscular system: peripheral nerve conduction velocity changes — heat increases it in sensory nerves; combined with reduced muscle-spindle and Golgi tendon organ discharge, muscle spindle excitability falls → decreased muscle spasm/guarding and reduced tone in spastic or painful muscle guarding; plus a sedative comfort effect on sensory endings.
  • Neuromuscular — pain relief operates via the gate-control mechanism (heat input through Aβ afferents closing the dorsal-horn gate) and by direct counter-irritant effects.
  • Connective tissue: increased collagen extensibility — the crucial effect in MSK physiotherapy: collagenous structures (capsule, tendon, ligament, scar) are best mobilised/stretched while heated, and the gain is maintained only if the stretch is held during cooling.
  • Joint and synovium: decreased joint stiffness (reduced viscosity of synovial fluid gels — the waxy stiffness of a cooled joint melts with heat), improved articular cartilage nutrition via cyclic perfusion, and pain relief in chronic degenerative arthritis.
  • Haematological/immune: increased capillary exchange supports the delivery of antibodies and phagocytes to the heated region — supportive to tissue healing.
  • Applications in MSK: pain and spasm relief before stretching a contracted joint (post-traumatic stiffness, frozen shoulder), subacute/chronic low-back pain, tendinopathy (deep heat), delayed-onset muscle soreness, and before manual therapy/mobilisation.
  • Precautions/contraindications: over acute inflammation/bleeding, malignancy, ischaemic tissue, insensitive skin, and acute injury.

Heat rule: stretch while hot, hold while cooling — that is what makes the collagen gain permanent.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II Unit 10 — Electro Physics: (d) biophysical effects of heat and cold, (e) clinical decision making in selecting electro-modalities.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. F.A. Davis — physical agents/thermal therapy chapter (syllabus reference 10).
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. F.A. Davis — thermal agents and connective-tissue stretching sections.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier — body-temperature regulation, local and systemic responses to heat.
1010 marks

Explain the pathomechanics following TA rupture.

Full answer →

Cover normal Achilles mechanics, the rupture mechanism, then ankle-level and gait-level pathomechanics.

  • What earns marks: applied anatomy & normal mechanics — Achilles tendon, triceps surae, push-off (3 marks) · mechanism of rupture + the phase affected (1.5 marks) · pathomechanics at the ankle — torque, ROM, eccentrics (2.5 marks) · pathomechanics of gait — push-off loss + compensations (2.5 marks) · rehabilitation significance + diagram (0.5 mark). Structure it: mechanics → rupture mechanics → ankle pathomechanics → gait pathomechanics.
  • The triceps surae (gastrocnemius + soleus) converges into the tendo-Achilles (TA), the thickest, strongest tendon in the body (withstands ~4000 N in walking), inserting on the calcaneal tuberosity.
  • As the prime plantarflexor, it generates the propulsive push-off (terminal stance–pre-swing) — the A2 plantarflexor-knee power burst that vaults the body over the stance foot.
  • It works eccentrically after heel strike to control tibial advancement (ankle dorsiflexion) — the soleus is postural and active through most of stance.
  • It also contributes to the windlass mechanism and shock absorption through mid-stance, and to venous return via the calf pump.
  • Mechanism of rupture: typically in the 30–50-year-old 'weekend athlete' — a sudden, violent eccentric contraction on a dorsiflexing ankle (landing from a jump or a push-off burst), often in a degenerated, hypovascular mid-tendon (watershed 2–6 cm above the insertion).
  • Patients report being 'hit in the calf by a stone'. Thompson's test (Simmonds') is positive: absent ankle plantarflexion on calf squeeze.
  • Pathomechanics at the ankle — loss of plantarflexion torque: the calf's force is not transmitted to the calcaneus, so plantarflexion strength is profoundly reduced and isolated plantarflexion is performed only by the long toe flexors, peroneals, tibialis posterior and plantaris (if present).
  • Loss of eccentric control: after initial contact the unrestrained tibia advances on the talus, so dorsiflexion is excessive and uncontrolled — the foot slaps into a flatter loading pattern.
  • Heel-cord insufficiency: the calcaneus loses its posterior tether and rides slightly anteriorly/proximally; if treated non-operatively with a gap, the tendon heals elongated → permanent weakness; with malalignment the calcaneus assumes a more vertical position because the plantarflexor pull line is lost (the 'calcaneus-type' deformity in chronic neglected rupture).
  • Arch and shock absorption: a diminished triceps surae contribution to the longitudinal arch mechanism alters mid-foot load sharing, increasing forefoot and medial-arch stress.
  • Gait — absent push-off / flat-foot gait: no heel rise, no terminal-stance plantarflexion power (loss of the A2 burst) — the affected step is shorter, with reduced or absent ankle plantarflexion at pre-swing.
  • Gait — compensatory pattern: hip flexion and hip-hiking with a shorter contralateral step; the patient 'walks through' the limb rather than over it; often an ipsilateral trunk lean and early hip-extensor substitution — the classic shift of propulsion from ankle to hip strategy.
  • Gait — stance-phase effects: decreased terminal-stance ankle plantarflexion moment, excessive dorsiflexion, reduced knee-extension moment → genu recurvatum avoidance patterns and increased demand on knee extensors; walking speed and cadence drop and energy cost per metre rises.
  • Functional losses: inability to do a single-limb heel raise, difficulty with stairs, running and jumping; altered venous return (calf-pump loss) → distal oedema risk.
  • Rehabilitation significance: pathomechanics dictates protocol — protect (equinus cast/orthosis in plantarflexion, functional bracing allowing early controlled tensioning), then progressively restore soleus–gastrocnemius eccentric strength, calf-pump conditioning, and finally push-off power and plyometrics before return to sport.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II Unit 6 (lower extremity joints, soft tissues) and Unit 8 (normal and pathological gait).
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. — biomechanics of the ankle-foot complex.
  • Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. F.A. Davis — ankle-foot complex chapter.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier — lower leg, ankle and foot assessment (Thompson/Simmonds test) (syllabus reference 4).
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. F.A. Davis — Achilles tendon rupture rehabilitation sections.

Q1. Describe the role of assessment in diagnosis.

Full answer →

Show assessment as a reasoning process (history, hypotheses, tests, diagnosis, reassessment), not a list of tests.

  • What earns marks: Present the answer as a process — history, then hypotheses, then tests, then diagnosis, then reassessment · Use the words 'hypothesis' and 'differential' and actually apply them · Link every finding to the ICF (body function, activity, participation).
  • Definition: Assessment is the systematic collection of data about a patient's status.
  • Definition: Diagnosis is the label you reach after interpreting that data.
  • PT diagnosis: In physiotherapy, assessment ends in a physiotherapy (movement-system) diagnosis — a cluster of signs and symptoms naming the dysfunction the therapist is trained to treat.
  • Example: e.g. 'subacromial impingement with scapular dyskinesis'.
  • Link to medical diagnosis: The PT diagnosis is separate from, but always linked to, the medical diagnosis.
  • Subjective (history): demographic data, chief complaint (onset, location, duration, aggravating/easing factors), pain behaviour (24-hour pattern), functional limits, past history, medications, and red/yellow-flag screening.
  • Key fact: The history alone steers about 80% of the hypothesis list.
  • Objective examination: observation (posture, deformity, gait), palpation, active/passive and accessory ROM (PPIVMs, PAIVMs), strength (MMT), joint mobility and special tests, neuro screening (dermatomes, myotomes, DTRs), and functional measures.
  • Hypothesis-oriented process: Good assessment is not a checklist but a hypothetico-deductive cycle.
  • Steps: generate competing hypotheses from the history, design tests to confirm or refute each, commit to a working diagnosis, and reassess after each treatment.
  • Reference: This is Jones & Rivett's clinical-reasoning model.
  • ICF mapping: findings map to body structure/function (e.g. restricted flexion, weak abductors), activity (can't squat) and participation (can't work as a farmer).
  • Purpose of mapping: it defines both the treatment targets and the outcome measures used for reassessment.
  • Assessment does five things: (i) establishes a baseline, (ii) enables differential diagnosis and red-flag screening for referral, (iii) guides treatment selection, (iv) measures change, and (v) gives the legal/professional documentation of autonomous practice.
  • Safety: red flags are screened at EVERY step.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 1 & 6.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier (syllabus reference 4).
  • Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. (reference 2)
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. (standard clinical-reasoning text)

Q2. Describe the screening of neck following C3-C4 disc prolapse.

Full answer →

Anchor every neurological line to C3/C4 — the high-collar dermatome, the shrug myotome, and 'no C4 reflex, test C5/C6'.

  • What earns marks: Anchor every neurological finding to C3/C4 — a generic neck exam loses marks · Draw the C3-C4 'high-collar' dermatome map with the myotome, reflex and special tests beside it · Name the red flags and finish with a clear conclusion.
  • Core idea: A C3-C4 prolapse usually compresses the C4 nerve root.
  • Pain pattern: pain in the suboccipital/neck region radiating to the shoulder cap and clavicular area (C4 dermatome — a 'high-collar' distribution).
  • C3 referral: C3 gives occipital/sub-occipital referral.
  • History: ask about onset, trauma, posture/occupation (e.g. prolonged laptop flexion), and night pain.
  • Red flags: myelopathy signs (gait change, hand clumsiness, bowel/bladder), fever, weight loss, trauma.
  • Observation: forward head posture, loss of cervical lordosis, antalgic tilt.
  • Palpation: paraspinal muscle spasm/guarding, segmental tenderness at the C3-C4 level, upper trapezius trigger points.
  • ROM: flexion/extension, side-flexion, rotation — look for painful arcs and a capsular vs non-capsular pattern.
  • Provocation: extension combined with ipsilateral rotation reproduces radicular symptoms in the affected dermatome.
  • Segmental mobility: central and unilateral posterior-anterior glides (PAIVMs) at C3-C4 for stiffness vs pain; intersegmental movement testing (PPIVMs).
  • Myotome C4: scapular elevation (shoulder shrug) and diaphragm (C3-C5) — 'C3,4,5 keep the diaphragm alive'; test the resisted shrug.
  • Reflex: there is no pure C4 DTR — test the biceps jerk (C5) and brachioradialis (C6) to exclude adjacent-root involvement.
  • Sensation: pinprick/light touch over the neck, clavicle and upper shoulder cap.
  • Also: complete the upper-limb screen for a broader deficit pattern.
  • Special tests: Spurling's test (extension + ipsilateral rotation + axial compression — radicular reproduction).
  • Special tests: cervical distraction (relief is confirmatory), shoulder-abduction (bakery) relief sign, and ULNT/neurodynamic testing for mechanosensitivity.
  • Special tests: Hoffman's test for myelopathy; quadriceps/Babinski if cord signs are suspected.
  • Close: integrate findings into a working PT diagnosis and baseline (NDI — Neck Disability Index).
  • Close: refer urgently for MRI if myelopathy or red flags appear.

Myotome ladder: C5 abduct, C6 wrist extend, C7 elbow extend, C8 finger flex, T1 finger abduct; Spurling (compression) pairs with distraction (relief).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2a.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier (reference 4) — cervical spine chapter.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1)
