Explain the mechanics and pathomechanics of non-specific neck pain.

Full answer →

Define "non-specific" first, then show the load-versus-capacity mechanics of the forward head and the chain of creep and motor-control change that produces the pain.

  • What earns marks: "non-specific" is the trap word. Define the term — no fracture, no tumour, no radiculopathy. Do NOT list disc prolapses and radiculopathy; those are specific · show the load-versus-capacity mechanics — the forward-head moment arm story · name the pathomechanical chain: creep, sustained postures, motor control change.
  • Normal mechanics: the cervical spine is a lordotic mobile column carrying a head of about four and a half to five kilograms.
  • The lordosis is not decoration: it places the compressive load closer to the axes of the posterior muscles and the uncovertebral joints, distributing stress.
  • Functionally it is two regions — the craniovertebral complex for nodding and rotation, and the mid and lower cervical segments for combined movements.
  • Coupling rule: side-flexion in the mid and lower cervical spine is classically coupled with rotation to the same side. This rule is broken only at the craniovertebral joints, where rotation is coupled with slight opposite side-flexion.
  • Motion segments each contribute roughly 13–23 degrees of flexion-extension on in-vivo studies, with the mid-cervical levels (C4–C5/C5–C6) among the most mobile — which is why degeneration shows there first.
  • Loading: in neutral, the head's centre of mass sits almost over the cervical column and the extensor moment arm is small.
  • Every centimetre the head drifts forward lengthens the horizontal moment arm of that five-kilogram head, so the extensor force must multiply to balance it — the biomechanics of the computer-and-mobile posture, which now includes young adults with text-neck patterns.
  • The flexion moment also loads the posterior elements, capsules and intervertebral discs eccentrically.
  • Pathomechanics: sustained static flexion imposes a constant load on viscoelastic tissue, and creep follows — ligaments and the posterior annulus lengthen under a load they were built to carry only briefly.
  • Recovery lags minutes to hours behind the insult; repeated daily, microstrain accumulates in poorly vascularised tissue.
  • The deep neck flexors (longus capitis and colli) become inhibited while the superficial sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius take over, so the segment loses its fine local control.
  • Proprioception from fatigued cervical muscles degrades, and the patient now holds posture by passive structures rather than active control.
  • Nociception from ligament, disc and muscle triggers protective spasm and referred pain over the scapula.
  • Nothing here is structurally "specific" — no fracture, no tumour, no radiculopathy — yet the mechanics fully explain the pain, which is precisely why the question says non-specific.
  • Treatment reverses the chain: posture re-education shrinks the moment arm; micro-breaks every 20–30 minutes outlast creep recovery; deep neck flexor training restores the local control the superficial muscles stole.
  • McKenzie's assessment of directional preference — often retraction and extension in postural syndromes — tests which movement re-centres the segment.
  • Conclusion: non-specific neck pain is a load-management problem — the tissues are normal, the dose they receive is not.

Non-specific neck pain is a load-management problem — the tissues are normal, the dose they receive is not.

Sources
  • McKenzie and May, The Cervical and Thoracic Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy — directional preference and postural syndromes.
  • Levangie and Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — cervical coupled motion and loading.
  • Butler and Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System — mechanosensitivity in persistent pain.
710 marks

How would you distinguish the mechanics and pathomechanics of the anterior cruciate ligament of the knee?

Full answer →

Contrast how the ACL works when intact with how the knee misbehaves after injury, and close with the clinical tests.

  • What earns marks: "distinguish" is the operative verb. Structure your answer as a two-column comparison — how the ligament behaves intact versus after injury · close with the Lachman test and the pivot-shift mechanism · keep mechanism (how it tore) separate from pathomechanics (how the knee misbehaves afterwards) — that distinction is exactly what the question tests.
  • Structure: the ACL runs from the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle down to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia.
  • That oblique course makes it the primary restraint to anterior tibial translation — it provides about 85 percent of that restraint — and a secondary restraint to rotation and hyperextension.
  • Mechanoreceptors within the ACL feed the CNS (Hilton's law), so ACL injury damages not just stability but reflex control.
  • Two functional bundles: the anteromedial (AM) bundle, taut in flexion, and the posterolateral (PL) bundle, taut in extension. This reciprocal tensioning keeps some fibres loaded throughout the arc.
  • Terminal extension holds the screw-home mechanism: as the knee locks, the tibia externally rotates on the femur, and the ACL winds up and tightens.
  • Pathomechanics — the classic non-contact mechanism: deceleration with the foot planted; the femur internally rotates and adducts over a fixed tibia with the knee near 20 degrees of flexion — valgus collapse.
  • The lateral tibial plateau subluxes anteriorly under the lateral femoral condyle and reduces with a clunk as the knee extends — the pivot shift episode, often remembered by the patient as "it went out and came back".
  • Hyperextension injuries and direct blows, as on a two-wheeler, tear it by other routes.
  • A partial tear leaves the checkrein intact; a complete tear removes anterior restraint, so the quadriceps — pulling up the slope of the tibial plateau — now drags the tibia forward on every attempted extension under load.
  • Consequences: episodes of giving way on pivoting, Indian-style squatting and cross-legged sitting, stairs and uneven roads.
  • Secondary meniscal and chondral damage from repeated subluxation; arthrogenic inhibition weakening the quadriceps; accelerated osteoarthritis; and lost proprioceptive acuity delaying protective reflexes further.
  • The ligament does not heal to functional competence because synovial fluid bathes the torn ends — a one-line justification for why conservative care must build muscle instead of waiting for the ligament.
  • Bedside test: the Lachman test — knee near 30 degrees, anterior drawer of the tibia — is the most sensitive clinical test and should be named first.
  • The pivot-shift test is the most specific though hardest to elicit in a guarded patient; the instrumented arthrometer quantifies the translation.

Mechanism is how it tore; pathomechanics is how the knee misbehaves afterwards.

Sources
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — Lachman, pivot shift and arthrometer testing.
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — ACL restraint and knee kinematics.
  • Donatelli and Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — rehabilitation after ACL injury.
810 marks

Explain the mechanism of control of posture.

Full answer →

Structure the answer as input, integration and output — the three sensory streams, the central hierarchy and the postural strategies.

  • What earns marks: structure the answer as input, integration, output — the three words examiners subconsciously tick · add the feed-forward versus feedback distinction — most candidates know only the reactive side, and that one sentence often separates the grades · give the latency hierarchy numbers — spinal 30–50 ms, long loop 100–150 ms, voluntary beyond 200 ms.
  • Definition: postural control is the continuous regulation of the body's centre of mass over its base of support.
  • In standing it is an inverted pendulum that would topple were it not corrected several times a second.
  • The continual small corrections appear as postural sway — sway itself is the measurable proof that control exists; perfectly rigid posture would mean falling, not standing.
  • Distinguish static control (quiet standing) from dynamic control (maintaining equilibrium while moving). Dynamic is the one our MSK and neurological patients struggle with most.
  • Sensory input 1 — visual: supplies a stable external reference, though an inaccurate one when the environment itself moves.
  • Sensory input 2 — vestibular: gives head position and acceleration.
  • Sensory input 3 — somatosensory: pressure on the soles, joint and muscle afferents. It is the dominant stream on firm ground.
  • The CNS weights the three according to context: on a compliant bus floor the somatosensory stream lies, so weighting shifts toward vision and the labyrinth; in the dark, vision is withdrawn and the remainder must cope.
  • This sensory re-weighting is why Romberg's test works: remove vision, and a somatosensory or vestibular deficit is unmasked.
  • Central integration is a hierarchy, not a switchboard: spinal circuits generate the fastest, crudest corrections.
  • The brainstem (vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts) manages the antigravity set against perturbation; the cerebellum calibrates and updates them; the basal ganglia select the strategy; the cortex overrides everything for voluntary, anticipatory control.
  • Latency tells the hierarchy apart: spinal reflexes act within roughly 30–50 milliseconds, long-loop corrections within about 100–150, and voluntary corrections beyond 200. Knowing these orders of magnitude helps interpret delayed balance reactions after stroke.
  • Motor output — anticipatory (feed-forward) postural adjustments prepare the body before movement: lift your arm and the trunk and leg muscles fire before the deltoid does.
  • Reactive (feedback) strategies correct unexpected displacement and scale with the size of the threat: the ankle strategy for small sway on a firm surface, the hip strategy for larger or faster displacement, and a step or a grasping arm when the base itself is exceeded.
  • Older adults, neuropathic feet and post-operative patients drift from ankle toward hip and stepping strategies — the physiological story behind the falls that fill our OPDs.
  • Clinical application: assessment maps to the mechanism — quiet stance with eyes open and closed on firm and compliant surfaces (the clinical sensory-organisation test), limits-of-stability and reaction to external perturbation.
  • Training follows the same map — challenge each sensory stream, then train each strategy under progressively harder conditions.
  • Conclusion: postural control is a closed sensorimotor loop, and every fall we prevent is a loop we repaired.

Sensors, processor, actuators — input, integration, output.

Sources
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — standing posture and equilibrium.
  • Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — vestibular and motor control hierarchy.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — balance assessment and training.
910 marks

Discuss the specific pain states and syndromes in musculoskeletal conditions.

Full answer →

Classify pain by mechanism, name each specific state with one discriminating clinical feature, and attach a treatment direction to each syndrome.

  • What earns marks: the word "specific" invites you to be precise — name each state with one discriminating clinical feature (morning stiffness over an hour, dermatomal versus non-dermatomal, claudication distance), and attach a treatment direction to each syndrome · classify pain by mechanism (nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic), not by body part · cite gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965) and the neuromatrix (Melzack, 1999) briefly.
  • Nociceptive pain arises from actual or threatened tissue damage — the sprained ankle, the arthritic knee. It is usually proportional, mechanical and well localised.
  • Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease of the nervous system itself — radicular pain, peripheral neuropathy.
  • Nociplastic pain arises from altered nociception without clear tissue or nerve damage: the nervous system has turned its own gain up.
  • Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965) and Melzack's later neuromatrix (1999) explain how modulation — spinal gating, descending inhibition, brain-body maps — lets the same input hurt differently in different people.
  • Acute pain is protective, time-limited and proportional; it resolves with healing.
  • Chronic pain — beyond three months — outlives healing and, in the International Association for the Study of Pain's framing, has become a disorder in its own right.
  • Inflammatory pain: rest and night pain, morning stiffness over about an hour and swelling — think rheumatoid, not osteoarthritis.
  • Ischaemic pain — claudication — is brought on by walking and relieved by standing still in under ten minutes; it must not be confused with night cramps.
  • Referred pain is felt remote from its source but is non-dermatomal and deep — a hip referring to the knee.
  • Radicular pain follows a dermatome and often has lancinating qualities — a C6 or L5 root.
  • Myofascial pain syndrome: a taut band with a focal trigger point that reproduces the patient's pain on pressure and refers in a characteristic pattern, with a local twitch response on snapping palpation.
  • Fibromyalgia: widespread pain for over three months with fatigue and non-restorative sleep, diagnosed on widespread distribution and symptom severity, commonly accompanied by central sensitisation — allodynia, hyperalgesia and spread beyond any tissue story.
  • Complex regional pain syndrome: disproportionate regional pain with sensory, vasomotor (colour and temperature change), sudomotor (sweating, oedema) and motor or trophic findings, classically after a minor limb injury or immobilisation — a familiar complication of an over-cautiously splinted Colles fracture.
  • Whiplash-associated disorder sits in the same spectrum of persistent MSK pain with sensitisation features.
  • Screen every persistent MSK patient for the pattern: pain disproportionate to findings, spread beyond one region, allodynia, poor response to tissue-directed treatment, and distress (the yellow flags of fear-avoidance and catastrophising). Pain drawings and simple questionnaires document it.
  • Treatment must match the mechanism: nociceptive pain responds to tissue-directed manual therapy and graded loading; neuropathic to pharmacological co-management and desensitisation; nociplastic and syndromic pain to pain neuroscience education, graded activity and exercise in dosages that do not flare the system.
  • Conclusion: we classify pain by mechanism because the mechanism, not the region, dictates the treatment.

Load the tissue OR calm the system.

Sources
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965.
  • Melzack R. From the gate to the neuromatrix. Pain 1999.
  • Butler and Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System — neuropathic and sensitisation states.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — chronic pain management.

Explain the biophysical effects of heat in adhesive capsulitis.

Full answer →

Describe heat's four biophysical effects, choose a modality deep enough for the capsule, and show the sequence heat-then-stretch with honest dosage and precautions.

  • What earns marks: the marking heart is sequence and honesty — heat first, stretch at the heated barrier, and admit that the stretch, not the heat, produces the range. Claiming heat alone cures a frozen shoulder loses the application marks · name the four effect families — vascular, metabolic, neural, connective tissue · choose the depth — the capsule is deep, so ultrasound or shortwave, not just a hot pack.
  • Raising tissue temperature produces four effect families, each with a physiotherapy use.
  • Vascular effects: vasodilatation and increased blood flow, which improves nutrition and clears metabolites.
  • Metabolic effects: tissue metabolic rate rises roughly 10–13 percent for every degree Celsius — healing and enzymatic repair accelerate.
  • Neural effects: warmth alters nerve conduction and, through the gate mechanism of Melzack and Wall, produces analgesia — large-fibre thermal input closing the gate on small-fibre pain.
  • Muscle spindle and gamma activity quietens, so muscle spasm eases.
  • Connective tissue effects: heated collagen becomes more extensible — and, the effect that matters in this question, elongation produced while the tissue is heated is retained after cooling, where the same stretch applied to cold tissue largely recoils.
  • Superficial agents — hot packs, paraffin wax, infrared — heat skin and subcutaneous tissue to about 1–2 centimetres, warming the shoulder mostly by conduction from the surface.
  • Because the glenohumeral capsule lies deeper, deep heating is traditionally preferred: shortwave diathermy at 27.12 MHz, and therapeutic ultrasound (which heats at the 3–5 centimetre depth of the capsule and can be focused on the coracohumeral ligament and anterior capsule).
  • In the thawing or frozen stage, where the capsule is the contractured tissue, the depth of the agent is the first clinical decision.
  • Adhesive capsulitis is, mechanically, a capsular contracture with pain-guarded loss of external rotation and abduction.
  • Heat is the preparation, not the cure: heat the capsule for 15–20 minutes, then apply grade II–IV mobilisations and sustained stretching to the barrier in the restricted directions — external rotation, abduction, internal rotation behind the back.
  • Heated collagen lengthens under less force, so the same stretch gains more and holds it; analgesia and reduced spasm raise the patient's tolerance, letting you work closer to the true barrier.
  • Controlled comparisons of combined heat-and-stretch programmes report better range gain than stretch alone — Lehmann's classic principle that tissue heated before stretch retains its elongation.
  • Dosage: hot packs 15–20 minutes, adequate towel layers, checking skin in insensate or diabetic patients — a real concern in Indian OPDs where diabetic frozen shoulders abound.
  • Deep agents: ultrasound at about 1 MHz for the deeper capsule, avoiding direct bone contact; shortwave not used over cardiac pacemakers, metal implants, malignancy, pregnancy or acute inflammation with shortwave.
  • Conclusion: heat does not melt a frozen shoulder; it lowers the pain cost and raises the tissue's willingness to be stretched — the stretch and the exercise still do the mechanical work. Prescribed that way, heat is a valuable assistant, not the hero.

Heat before stretch — the stretch, not the heat, produces the range.

Sources
  • Kisner and Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — thermal agents and stretching of connective tissue.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — physical agents in rehabilitation.
  • Donatelli and Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — management of the stiff shoulder.

Q1. Explain in detail the basic assessment methods for diagnosis of musculoskeletal conditions.

Full answer →

Show you can move step by step from a patient's complaint to a physiotherapy diagnosis, in the right order, and say what each step is for.

  • What earns marks: keep the sequence visible — subjective → look → feel → move → special tests → synthesis. The examiner is marking your diagnostic reasoning, not the page count · quote the classic line that a carefully taken history alone gives roughly 80 per cent of the diagnosis · name one Indian occupational example in the history (for example, a farmer lifting sacks) to show contextual thinking.
  • The diagnostic ladder: every musculoskeletal diagnosis follows one fixed order — subjective examination, look, feel, move, special tests, then synthesis.
  • Why the order matters: each step either confirms or removes a hypothesis, so no time is wasted on tests that cannot change your decision.
  • Subjective examination: start with age and sex (degenerative disease in the elderly, inflammatory arthropathy in the young adult), occupation, and hand dominance.
  • Pain history: record the mechanism (trauma versus insidious onset) and analyse the pain — site, onset, character, radiation, aggravating and relieving factors, behaviour over 24 hours, and night pain.
  • Past history: past medical history (diabetes, steroid use suggesting osteoporosis, previous surgery), drug history, and family history.
  • Inspection (look): posture standing and sitting, gait, deformity, swelling, muscle wasting (compare sides — supraspinatus fossa, thenar eminence, quadriceps above the patella), skin colour, scars and sinuses.
  • Palpation (feel): a systematic order — skin temperature, swelling, then bony and soft-tissue tenderness — always comparing with the unaffected side.
  • Movement (move): test in a fixed order — active range first, then passive range (note the end-feel: capsular, bony, springy block, empty), then resisted isometric testing.
  • Cyriax's rule at the bedside: pain on active and resisted movement but not passive suggests contractile tissue; pain reproduced only passively suggests inert structures — capsule, ligament, joint.
  • Special tests: only after the basic examination, and chosen, not sprayed — pick the tests that separate your top two or three hypotheses.
  • Functional and dynamic assessment: gait analysis, squatting, stair negotiation, a timed up-and-go — because function, not range, is what the patient actually complains of.
  • Adjuncts: when findings are inconclusive or systemic disease is suspected — plain radiographs, MRI, ultrasound, laboratory studies and electrodiagnosis.
  • Screening role: physical assessment doubles as a screen of neighbouring regions — a shoulder pain deserves a cervical screen, a knee pain deserves a hip and foot screen.
  • Synthesis: cluster the findings; the subjective and objective data must fit each other, then state a physiotherapy diagnosis at the level of impairment and function (for example, "subacromial pain syndrome with restricted and painful elevation and scapular dyskinesia").
  • Differential diagnosis: commit to a ranked short list of other conditions that could produce the same presentation, each one eliminated by a named finding.
  • Close the loop: document baseline measures, set goals, and plan re-assessment — a diagnosis that is never re-tested is only an opinion.

Subjective → Look → Feel → Move → Special tests → Synthesis; history alone gives about 80 per cent of the diagnosis.

Sources

  • Nordin M, Frankel VH — Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System (ref 1): tissue response framework.
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA — Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice: hypothesis generation and testing.

Q2. Elaborate the assessment method with differential diagnosis for shoulder impingement syndrome.

Full answer →

Give the mechanism, the special-test battery with its accuracy numbers, and the differential diagnosis, then cluster the findings into the diagnosis.

  • What earns marks: quote the pooled numbers — Neer about 0.79 sensitivity and 0.53 specificity — and say what they mean: a sensitive screen but a poor confirmer, so use a cluster of tests · draw the painful arc with two dashed lines at 60 and 120 degrees and label it · name the red flag — a Pancoast tumour presenting as shoulder pain with hand wasting and Horner syndrome in a smoker.
  • What is pinched: the subacromial space lies between the coracoacromial arch above (acromion, coracoacromial ligament, AC joint) and the humeral head with its rotator cuff below.
  • Structures that can be compressed: the supraspinatus tendon, the subacromial bursa, and the intra-articular portion of the long head of biceps.
  • Neer's stages: stage I — oedema and haemorrhage in the young overhead athlete; stage II — fibrosis and tendinopathy in the 25–40 age group; stage III — bone spurs and partial or complete cuff tears above 40.
  • Primary versus secondary: primary impingement comes from intrinsic tendon degeneration or a hooked acromion; secondary impingement is driven by glenohumeral instability or scapular dyskinesia letting the head ride up — the treatment differs completely.
  • Typical patient: an overhead worker (a painter, a batsman, a housewife lifting pots onto a high shelf) with pain over the deltoid insertion, painful overhead reaching, and night pain when lying on the affected side.
  • Inspection: forward-head rounded-shoulder posture, a prominent inferior angle of the scapula, scapular dyskinesia on repeated elevation (the "shrug" sign), and wasting of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae (which suggests a chronic cuff tear).
  • Neer test: scapula stabilised, arm passively flexed in internal rotation; pooled sensitivity around 0.8 but specificity only around 0.5.
  • Hawkins-Kennedy test: 90° flexion with forced internal rotation; similar accuracy — a sensitive screen, not a confirmer.
  • Painful arc: pain between roughly 60 and 120 degrees of active abduction; more specific — note whether it is present in passive abduction too.
  • Cuff tests: the Jobe empty-can position for supraspinatus strength, resisted external rotation for infraspinatus, and an external rotation lag or drop-arm test — true weakness out of proportion to pain points towards a tear rather than impingement.
  • Scapular assistance test: if symptoms improve when you assist the scapula upward, dyskinesia is a driver and rehabilitation must include scapular retraining.
  • Differential — cervical radiculopathy C5–C6: pain and paraesthesia below the elbow, worse with neck movement, positive Spurling test; always clear the cervical spine in every shoulder case.
  • Differential — adhesive capsulitis: global restriction of both active and passive external rotation and abduction, not just a painful arc; AC arthritis: pain on top of the joint, positive cross-body adduction test.
  • Other differentials: calcific tendinitis (dramatic night pain, confirmed on radiograph), glenohumeral osteoarthritis (crepitus and a capsular pattern), superior labral (SLAP) lesion (deep click, positive biceps load test), rotator cuff tear (persistent lag and true weakness), suprascapular neuropathy (isolated fossa wasting without a painful arc).
  • Conclusion: a consistent history of overhead pain with night pain, a positive Neer and Hawkins, a painful arc and preserved strength cluster into subacromial impingement syndrome with scapular contribution.
  • Escalation: persistent pure weakness or a positive lag test upgrades the suspicion to a cuff tear and warrants ultrasound or MRI referral.
  • Management: begin with a three-month structured conservative trial — scapular control, posterior capsule mobility, rotator cuff loading — before any question of subacromial decompression is raised.

Neer stages I–III: under 25 oedema, 25–40 fibrosis, over 40 spurs and tears; painful arc 60–120°; persistent weakness or lag sign = think cuff tear.

  • Hawkins RJ, Kennedy JC — Am J Sports Med, 1980: the impingement test.
  • Hertling D, Kessler RM — Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders (ref 15): impingement rehabilitation.

Q3. How do you conclude while screening that the pain in the lumbar spine is due to disc herniation? Justify with differential diagnosis.

Full answer →

Show how you combine several findings into a cluster — never one sign — to conclude disc herniation, and name the single test that separates each mimic.

  • What earns marks: the question asks "how do you conclude", so write a decision, not a description — state the four-point cluster, then one line per differential with its single discriminating test · quote SLR sensitivity 0.91 / specificity 0.26 and crossed SLR 0.28 / 0.90 — this converts a pass answer into a distinction answer · name the cauda equina red flag — bowel-bladder change with saddle anaesthesia is a same-day surgical referral, not an exercise prescription.
  • Mechanism: the posterior longitudinal ligament reinforces the disc centrally, so herniations track posterolaterally, exactly where the nerve root lies.
  • Levels: over 90 per cent occur at L4–L5 (compressing L5) and L5–S1 (compressing S1).
  • Pain profile: younger adult, 20–50 years; flexion- and sitting-intolerant pain (sitting raises intradiscal pressure roughly 40 per cent above standing); pain radiating below the knee in a dermatomal band — true sciatica, not the vague thigh ache of referred pain.
  • Relief: often in supine lying or standing extension. Symptoms arise from both mechanical deformation and chemical inflammation of the dorsal root ganglion, which is why leg pain severity can outrun the MRI appearance.
  • Neurological screening (the three-legged stool): screen dermatomes, myotomes and reflexes on both sides.
  • Sensation: L4 over the medial malleolus, L5 over the dorsum of the first web space, S1 over the lateral foot.
  • Motor: ankle dorsiflexion (L4), great-toe extension (L5), ankle plantarflexion and rising on toes (S1) — as resisted isometric holds, graded side to side.
  • Reflexes: knee jerk (L4) and ankle jerk (S1); L5 has no reliable reflex, so great-toe extension weakness plus an absent ankle jerk localises cleanly. A reproducible, side-to-side-documented deficit is the strongest evidence that the pain is radicular, not merely referred.
  • SLR: tensions the L5 and S1 roots; the classic pooled values (Deville et al., meta-analysis, Spine 2000) are sensitivity about 0.91 with specificity only about 0.26 — excellent for ruling out when negative, poor for ruling in.
  • Crossed SLR: sensitivity about 0.28 but specificity near 0.90, so a positive crossed SLR is close to confirmatory.
  • Add the slump test for sensitivity, and sensitizers (ankle dorsiflexion and cervical flexion) to prove the pain is neurogenic rather than hamstring or sacroiliac.
  • Centralisation: pain withdrawing from the foot towards the spine during repeated movement testing is a further discogenic pointer.
  • The concluding cluster: leg-dominant pain in a dermatomal band below the knee, plus at least one objective neurological deficit (sensory change, myotomal weakness or an absent reflex), plus a positive neurodynamic test, with symptom centralisation on movement testing.
  • When all four converge, state: "lumbar disc herniation with L5 (or S1) radiculopathy" — naming the level is the justification the question demands. If the cluster is incomplete, say what is missing: a positive SLR without any deficit behaves like discogenic pain without root compression, which usually has a better prognosis.
  • Differential — facet joint arthropathy: extension- and rotation-provoked localised back pain, no leg deficit. Sacroiliac joint pain: pain over the posterior superior iliac spine, positive Laslett cluster, negative SLR. Piriformis/deep gluteal syndrome: sciatica-like pain with a tender piriformis, SLR often positive but slump negative.
  • Differential — hip osteoarthritis: groin pain, restricted internal rotation, pain on FABER. Spinal stenosis: leg symptoms that ease on flexion and walking uphill in an older patient (the mirror image of discogenic flexion intolerance). Peripheral diabetic neuropathy: glove-and-stocking, symmetrical, non-dermatomal.
  • Red flag screen before any of this: age under 20 or over 55 with new pain, night pain unrelieved by position, fever, weight loss, trauma, cancer history, steroid use, or any bowel-bladder change with saddle anaesthesia.
  • Order imaging only for red flags or when invasive treatment is planned — a sizeable minority of asymptomatic adults show disc herniation on MRI, so imaging must correlate with the clinical cluster, not replace it.

SLR 0.91/0.26 and crossed SLR 0.28/0.90 — rule out versus rule in; L4–L5 hits L5, L5–S1 hits S1, and L5 has no reflex (use great-toe extension).

Sources
  • Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4), lumbar spine chapter.
  • Levangie PK, Norkin CC — Joint Structure and Function (ref 2): disc mechanics and loading.
  • Deville WLJM et al. — Spine, 2000: pooled accuracy of SLR (meta-analysis).
  • Laslett M et al. — Manual Therapy, 2005: sacroiliac cluster, used here for differential discrimination.

Q4. Discuss autonomous practice and the decision-making process in musculoskeletal physiotherapy.

Full answer →

Show the decision architecture — the models of reasoning, the screening duty, the referral trigger — not just a list of treatment techniques.

  • What earns marks: marks live in the decision architecture — models of reasoning, the screening obligation, the referral trigger — not in a list of treatment techniques · give one concrete Indian scenario (for example, an undiagnosed diabetic presenting as foot pain) to show applied autonomy rather than textbook recall.
  • Autonomous practice means the physiotherapist works as a first-contact, primary-care professional: the patient may arrive without a physician referral.
  • The physiotherapist independently performs the examination, decides whether the problem belongs in physiotherapy or outside it, makes the diagnosis at the level of impairment and function, and sets the plan of care — accepting full professional accountability.
  • Direct access is the enabling mechanism; in India, referral requirements are not uniform — several states and institutional settings allow patients to approach physiotherapy directly, and musculoskeletal physiotherapists increasingly run first-contact clinics in metros.
  • Decision model 1 — hypothetico-deductive: the novice pathway; from the first cues you build a hypothesis list, test each with selected questions and tests, and revise until one survives — slow, conscious and safe.
  • Decision model 2 — pattern recognition: the expert shortcut; thousands of stored illness scripts let the clinician match the presentation almost at sight — fast, but vulnerable to atypical presentations and bias.
  • Decision model 3 — dual-process theory: System 1 is the fast intuitive match, System 2 the slow analytic check; expertise is knowing when to switch, especially when the pattern fit is imperfect or the patient is not responding as expected.
  • Errors in musculoskeletal practice are rarely knowledge errors — they are reasoning errors (premature closure and confirmation bias), so the deliberate use of "what else could this be?" is a professional skill.
  • Screening obligation: because no physician has pre-screened the patient, every musculoskeletal assessment under direct access begins with a medical screen.
  • What to screen for: red flags of serious spinal pathology; medical mimics (claudication presenting as calf pain, diabetic neuropathy presenting as foot pain, visceral referral presenting as thoracic or shoulder pain); medications (long-term steroids, anticoagulants, bisphosphonates); and baseline vital signs when the history warrants.
  • The screen is not a one-time event: a patient who fails to improve as expected at two or three visits is re-screened, because non-response is itself a red flag for a wrong diagnosis.
  • Indian reality sharpens this duty: patients may arrive self-medicated, with undiagnosed diabetes or tuberculosis, and with late presentations — the autonomous physiotherapist is often the first health professional to notice the weight loss behind a "backache".
  • Referral: refer urgently when red flags appear — suspected fracture, malignancy, infection, cauda equina, acute inflammatory arthritis.
  • Refer for medical opinion when the presentation is outside your differential, when the patient deteriorates, or when expected improvement does not occur within the agreed number of sessions.
  • Within musculoskeletal practice you decide the pathway: classification-based treatment (for example, a treatment-based classification for low back pain), manual therapy versus exercise direction, and progression criteria governed by re-assessment rather than habit.
  • Legal and ethical face of autonomy: informed consent before assessment and treatment, truthfulness about the limits of your competence, record-keeping that would survive scrutiny, and honesty about prognostic uncertainty.
  • The defensible position: "I referred because I was not sure" is a defensible decision; "I treated because I did not check" is not.
  • Documentation: document the reasoning, not just the findings — what you suspected, what you tested, what you concluded, and why the referral was or was not made.
  • Anchor progress with validated outcome measures so continuation of care is justified by data, and maintain competence through continuing education and clinical audit — autonomous practice is a licence granted to a professional who keeps proving it.

Novice = hypothetico-deductive; expert = pattern recognition; wisdom = knowing when to switch. Red-flag screen on day one AND whenever the patient fails to improve as expected.

Sources
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA — Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice: dual-process theory and clinical patterns.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ — Physical Rehabilitation (ref 10): clinical decision making in physical therapy.
  • Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4): screening principles in the introduction.

Q5. Distinguish the various special tests with interpretation for knee instability.

Full answer →

Distinguish the tests with contrast — give each a one-line accuracy figure and say what it is for (to detect, to confirm, or to grade).

  • What earns marks: the verb is "distinguish", so never present the tests as a list without contrast — give each a one-line accuracy figure and say what it is for (Lachman to detect, pivot shift to confirm, drawer to grade in chronic knees) · write "an acute haemarthrosis within two hours of a pivot injury is ACL until proven otherwise" · name the Ottawa knee rules as the clinical screen for when a radiograph is actually needed.
  • Definition: ligamentous instability is abnormal translation or rotation of the tibia on the femur, and you classify it by direction.
  • Types: straight instabilities (anterior, posterior, medial, lateral) versus combined or rotatory instabilities (anteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral).
  • Mechanism predicts the torn structure: a non-contact pivot (valgus load with the foot planted and the body rotating — the classic kabaddi or football cutting injury) ruptures the ACL.
  • A dashboard injury or a fall on a flexed knee with the foot planted drives the tibia backwards and ruptures the PCL; a blow to the lateral side opens the medial compartment and grades the MCL.
  • Lachman test (the workhorse): knee at 20–30 degrees of flexion, one hand stabilising the femur, the other drawing the tibia anteriorly; pooled sensitivity about 0.85 with specificity about 0.94.
  • Lachman end-feel matters: soft or mushy compared with the other side, with loss of the firm stop, is positive.
  • Anterior drawer at 90 degrees: more familiar but weaker in the acute knee (about 0.55 sensitivity) because hamstring guarding blocks the translation — more useful in chronic tears.
  • Pivot shift: under a valgus load the ACL-deficient knee subluxes anteriorly in extension and reduces with a clunk as it flexes; sensitivity is low, around 0.24, but specificity near 0.98 — a positive pivot shift is essentially confirmatory, so it is never your first test.
  • Posterior sag sign (Godfrey): supine, hips and knees flexed to 90 degrees supported by the examiner, and the tibia visibly drops backwards — a quiet, high-yield observation that is often missed.
  • Posterior drawer: the most sensitive PCL test (around 0.9); push the tibia posteriorly at 90 degrees and grade against the contralateral step-off of the medial tibial plateau.
  • Quadriceps active test: asking the seated patient to slide the foot forward fires the quadriceps and visibly pulls a posteriorly-sagged tibia back into place — a PCL tear written in front of your eyes.
  • Valgus and varus stress testing is done twice: at 30 degrees of flexion (which isolates the collateral because the cruciates are slack) and at full extension (where the capsule and both cruciates also contribute — laxity at 0 degrees means a more extensive injury).
  • Dial test at 30 and 90 degrees of flexion: increased external rotation at 30 degrees only = isolated posterolateral corner injury; increased at both angles = combined PCL plus posterolateral injury.
  • Rotatory tests such as the Slocum anteromedial drawer complete the picture for combined instabilities.
  • Ottawa knee rules (the radiograph screen): age, isolated patella tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, and inability to bear weight for four steps.
  • Grading grammar: grade I — pain with stress but no laxity; grade II — laxity with a firm endpoint; grade III — laxity with a soft or absent endpoint.
  • Cluster: mechanism plus acute haemarthrosis plus a positive Lachman with a soft endpoint is an ACL rupture; add a positive pivot shift and the rotatory instability is clinically significant.
  • A positive Lachman combined with laxity to valgus stress at 0 degrees signals a multi-ligament knee that needs urgent orthopaedic referral, not a programme sheet.
  • Instrumented arthrometry and MRI confirm and quantify when surgery is contemplated, but the clinical cluster remains the reference standard at the bedside.

Lachman 0.85/0.94 at 20–30°; pivot shift 0.24/0.98 — confirm, never screen; anterior drawer weak acutely. Valgus at 30° = MCL, at 0° = cruciate involved too; posterior sag = PCL.

Sources
  • Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4), knee chapter: ligament stress testing.
  • Torg JS, Conrad W, Kalen V — Clin Orthop Relat Res, 1976: the Lachman test.
  • Galway RD, Beaupré A, MacIntosh DL — Clin Orthop, 1972: the pivot shift phenomenon.
  • Stiell IG et al. — JAMA, 1996: Ottawa knee rules for radiography.

Q6. Explain exercise testing in musculoskeletal disease.

Full answer →

Show why you test, how you keep it safe (named contraindications and stop criteria), what you measure, and how the results write the prescription.

  • What earns marks: every answer must contain a named contraindication list and termination criteria — in many Indian clinics there is no crash trolley next to the physiotherapy department, and saying that shows you understand why the list exists · draw the test loop with the stop box and its four termination criteria visible.
  • Definition: exercise testing is the measurement of a patient's physical capacity under controlled, graded loading.
  • Three purposes in musculoskeletal practice: it quantifies the impairment (how weak, how unfit, how easily fatigued), it gives the baseline against which the whole rehabilitation programme is judged, and it is itself a motivational and educational tool — a patient who sees the number move believes in the treatment.
  • It also screens function beyond the index joint: the knee may be the complaint, but aerobic capacity and global strength determine whether the patient returns to work or the field.
  • Pre-test screening: take the cardiovascular history, use a structured self-report such as the PAR-Q+ as a first filter, measure baseline heart rate and blood pressure, and review medications.
  • A beta-blocker flattens the heart-rate response, so rating of perceived exertion becomes your gauge instead of pulse alone.
  • Absolute contraindications (stops): uncontrolled hypertension (above 180/110), unstable angina, recent infarction, uncontrolled arrhythmia, acute deep-vein thrombosis, acute inflammation or fever, and uncontrolled metabolic disease.
  • Relative contraindications (they modify the modality): significant musculoskeletal pain, recent surgery, and severe osteoporosis. Obtain informed consent and explain stop signals before you start.
  • Aerobic testing — maximal: graded exercise testing on a treadmill or cycle ergometer directly measures VO2max, but it is rarely needed in musculoskeletal clinics.
  • Aerobic testing — submaximal: the Åstrand-Rhyming or YMCA cycle protocols, or a treadmill test terminated at a target heart rate or an RPE of about 15, estimate VO2max from the heart-rate response.
  • Field tests for resource-limited settings: the six-minute walk test for endurance in elderly and post-operative patients, the two-minute walk or shuttle walk for higher-functioning patients, and the sit-to-stand test for lower-limb power in older adults. Record the mode, because numbers are not interchangeable across tests.
  • Strength hierarchy: manual muscle testing for grading 0–5 where weakness is marked, and handheld dynamometry for an objective force reading.
  • For prescribing progressive resistance: one-repetition maximum or its safer estimate from a 6–10 repetition maximum (the Brzycki equation); and isokinetic dynamometry where velocity-controlled torque data are needed.
  • Classic isokinetic use: the hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, conventionally about 0.6, with asymmetry beyond about 10 per cent between limbs flagged as a reinjury risk after ACL reconstruction.
  • Muscular endurance: measured by timed holds or repetition counts; functional composite tests (the timed up-and-go, stair climb, single-leg hop battery) translate muscle data into capability.
  • Interpretation: heart rate and blood pressure should rise together, and perceived exertion should track the load (Borg 6–20 scale, or CR10).
  • Absolute termination criteria: a falling blood pressure, angina, marked dyspnoea, dizziness, an abnormal gait, or RPE above 17.
  • Musculoskeletal interpretation: compare side-to-side symmetry of strength and endurance, and record the distance walked, the claudication or pain onset distance in osteoarthritis and vascular insufficiency, and the load tolerated.
  • The results write the prescription: intensity from the heart-rate reserve or RPE zone, volume from the repetition maximum, and progression by documented increments.
  • Re-test under identical conditions every few weeks — same time of day, same mode, same instructions — because only a comparable number can prove progress.

Stop criteria: BP drop, angina, RPE above 17, dizziness — memorise all four. Six-minute walk for endurance; 6–10 RM to estimate 1 RM; H:Q ratio about 0.6.

Sources
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ — Physical Rehabilitation (ref 10): exercise testing and prescription chapters.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH — Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System (ref 1): load-response principles.
  • Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4): functional testing of the lower limb.

Q7. Outline the orthotic devices with indications for spinal conditions.

Full answer →

Every device must earn its mark through a named indication — then add the limitations paragraph and the weaning plan.

  • What earns marks: the question says "with indications", so every device earns its mark only through a named indication · the examiner's test of depth is the limitations paragraph and the weaning plan — most students can list braces; fewer can say when to stop one.
  • Definition: an orthosis is an externally applied device that supports, aligns, prevents or corrects a body segment while improving function — distinguished from a prosthesis, which replaces a missing part.
  • Biomechanical principle 1 — the three-point pressure system: an anterior force balanced by two posterior counter-forces, or the reverse.
  • Other principles: distraction or offloading to reduce axial load on healing bone; motion restriction in selected planes (flexion is easiest to block, rotation hardest); and postural cueing by proprioceptive reminder.
  • Prescription follows the diagnosis, the stage of healing and the patient: a device that cannot be tolerated in a humid Indian summer will not be worn, and an unworn orthosis is a failed prescription.
  • Soft cervical collar: gives comfort and a reminder effect but almost no motion control — prescribe briefly for acute sprains and wean within one to two weeks to avoid dependency.
  • Philadelphia collar: two-piece foam with a plastic shell; restricts flexion-extension modestly — suitable for stable fractures and post-fusion support.
  • SOMI (sterno-occipital-mandibular-immobiliser): adds chin and occipital control with a sternal plate, better for flexion control, usable even in the supine patient with a headboard attachment; the Guilford four-poster adds similar control from a pelvic base.
  • Halo vest: a ring fixed to the skull by pins, attached to a vest — the most rigid cervical immobilisation, for unstable cervical fractures and post-operative fixation, but it demands pin-site care, so physiotherapy follow-up is mandatory.
  • Taylor and cruciform anterior hyperextension orthoses: a three-point system (a sternal pad and a pubic pad anteriorly, a thoracic pad posteriorly) creating an extension moment — for stable anterior compression fractures and posture support in healing kyphoplasty patients.
  • Jewett hyperextension brace: the same principle in a lighter, more tolerable frame, for stable thoracolumbar compression fractures, generally from about T8 to L3.
  • TLSO (thoracolumbosacral orthosis): custom-moulded or prefabricated, gives circumferential control of the trunk — after spinal fusion, for burst fractures with an intact posterior wall, and for situational offloading in osteoporotic patients.
  • The trade-off: better control costs greater discomfort, heat intolerance and trunk-muscle disuse, so the weaning plan is part of the prescription, not an afterthought.
  • Scoliosis bracing prevents progression of an immature curve, and the choice follows curve apex and maturity.
  • Milwaukee (cervico-thoracolumbosacral orthosis): the historic prototype with a neck ring and throat mould, still used for high thoracic curves with the apex above about T8.
  • Underarm TLSO (Boston-type): covers curves with apexes below T8, the commonest modern prescription, with full-time wear (16–23 hours) while the child grows, guided by the Risser sign — bracing helps until skeletal maturity, not after.
  • Charleston night-time bending brace: fabricated in maximal correction for single flexible thoracolumbar or lumbar curves; trades daytime freedom for night-only wear.
  • Bracing is prevention, not correction of an established structural curve — and the psychological load of full-time wear on a teenager is a clinical problem in itself, which is why counselling and sport continuation are part of the orthotic plan.
  • Lumbosacral corset: raises intra-abdominal pressure to offload the lumbar spine — for mechanical low back pain, symptomatic spondylolysis and listhesis, and post-operative support.
  • Sacroiliac belt: compresses the pelvic ring — for sacroiliac joint dysfunction, and commonly in India for pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain where it lets the mother keep working.
  • Limitations of all orthoses: prolonged rigid bracing weakens the trunk musculature it replaces, causes heat rash and pressure sores in our climate, may reduce bone density with long use, and can create psychological dependency.
  • Therefore prescribe with a defined duration, an exercise programme to maintain what the brace is resting, and a written weaning schedule.

Three-point pressure and extension moment explain Taylor, Jewett and TLSO at one stroke. Halo = unstable cervical; Jewett / TLSO = stable thoracolumbar; Milwaukee = apex above T8. Every brace needs one indication and one limitation; wean to prevent disuse.

Sources
  • Chui K, Jorge M, Yen S-C, Lusardi MM — Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation (ref 18): spinal orthoses chapters.
  • Maxey L, Magnusson JA — Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient (ref 13): post-operative bracing timelines.
  • McKinnis LN — Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging (ref 8): imaging follow-up of braced fractures.

Q8. Describe the assessment method for a two-year-old child who developed excessive lateral curvature of the thoracic spine.

Full answer →

Everything must flow from the age — infantile onset, Mehta's RVAD method, and the resolving-versus-progressive decision.

  • What earns marks: the age is the question — infantile onset, left thoracic male predominance, RVAD, Mehta phases and serial casting all flow from the child being two; any general scoliosis answer without Mehta's method reads as a missed question · draw the curved spine with the two end-vertebra lines and label the 10-degree threshold.
  • Frame the problem: a lateral curvature appearing up to three years of age is infantile idiopathic scoliosis; at two years it is early-onset scoliosis.
  • Separate it from three dangerous mimics: congenital scoliosis (a hemivertebra or failure of segmentation visible on radiographs, often linked with cardiac and renal anomalies).
  • Mimic 2 — neuromuscular scoliosis (cerebral palsy, myelodysplasia, spinal dysraphism — always confirmed or excluded by neurological examination); mimic 3 — syndromic scoliosis (neurofibromatosis, Marfan, muscle disease).
  • Birth history: breech delivery and first-born status associate with infantile idiopathic scoliosis; ask about milestones, a persistently tilted posture, a hump, an asymmetrical skin crease, and family history.
  • Clinical examination: examine on the mother's lap if the child will not cooperate, and undress adequately while keeping the room warm.
  • Inspect standing (if the child stands reliably) and sitting: shoulder level, scapular prominence, waist crease asymmetry, pelvic level and head position.
  • Adam's forward-bend test: shows a rib hump on the convex side of a structural thoracic curve — in a two-year-old, perform it across your lap and use a scoliometer if the child allows.
  • The screen most candidates forget — the skin: café-au-lait patches of neurofibromatosis, a hairy patch, dimple or sinus over the spine suggesting dysraphism.
  • Complete neurological examination: tone, gait if walking, muscle bulk and reflexes, and check the abdomen for a neurological bladder pattern.
  • Examine the hips (developmental dysplasia or an adduction contracture can produce a compensatory apparent curve) and measure leg lengths.
  • Infantile idiopathic scoliosis characteristically shows a left thoracic curve in a boy — a left thoracic curve at any age warrants the most thorough neurological screen.
  • Radiology: request a full-length posteroanterior spine radiograph (supine if standing films are impossible at this age) and read it systematically.
  • Cobb angle: the angle between the most tilted end vertebra above and below the curve, with 10 degrees the conventional diagnostic threshold for scoliosis.
  • Mehta's rib-vertebral angle difference (RVAD): draw a line perpendicular to the end plate of the apical vertebra and lines along the necks of the ribs on each side; an RVAD above about 20 degrees marks a curve at risk of progression.
  • Mehta's phase 2 — the rib head on the convex side overlapping the vertebral body — is a progression marker even at normal angles. Look specifically for congenital anomalies: hemivertebrae, bars, fused ribs.
  • Where neurological signs coexist, an MRI of the entire spine is indicated before any management decision.
  • Resolving versus progressive: the majority of infantile idiopathic curves — historically quoted at around 90 per cent — resolve spontaneously, especially double thoracic curves with a low RVAD.
  • Resolving pattern: flexible curve, RVAD under 20 degrees, rib phase 1, and no vertebral anomaly. Progressive pattern: single curve, RVAD above 20 degrees, phase 2 changes, and often early radiographic deterioration on serial films.
  • The determination is made by comparing measurements, which is why the first follow-up at about four months is part of assessment itself.
  • Management: resolving and low-risk curves are observed with radiographs every four to six months, with parental education on symmetry of carrying and play positioning.
  • Progressive curves are referred without delay to a paediatric orthopaedic spine surgeon — serial Mehta casting under anaesthesia (elongation-derotation-flexion), then bracing once walking age is established, with growth-friendly options such as magnetically controlled growing rods for severe curves.
  • Screen associated systems in congenital cases — echocardiography and renal ultrasound.
  • The physiotherapist's assessment output is therefore a classification: idiopathic-resolving, idiopathic-progressive, congenital, neuromuscular or syndromic — each with a different urgency of referral.

Under three = infantile idiopathic; left thoracic curve in a boy; most resolve spontaneously. Cobb 10° threshold; Mehta RVAD above 20° or rib phase 2 = progression risk.

Sources
  • McKinnis LN — Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging (ref 8): scoliosis measurement on radiographs.
  • Greenspan A, Beltran J — Orthopaedic Imaging: A Practical Approach (ref 9): congenital vertebral anomalies.
  • Mehta MH — J Bone Joint Surg Br, 1972: the rib-vertebral angle difference in infantile scoliosis.
  • Maxey L, Magnusson JA — Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient (ref 13): paediatric orthopaedic rehabilitation context.

Q9. Explain the pre- and post-operative assessment of fracture neck of femur.

Full answer →

Answer both halves equally — pre-operative and post-operative assessment — and show that the surgical choice (fixation versus arthroplasty) changes your assessment.

  • What earns marks: the question asks for both pre- AND post-operative assessment — split your answer visibly fifty-fifty; students who rush the pre-operative half cap themselves at half marks · say plainly that pre-operative teaching is physiotherapy assessment with a therapeutic intent · draw the timeline with the two weight-bearing tracks (fixation versus arthroplasty) beneath it.
  • Classification (Garden): types I and II are undisplaced (valgus impacted or incomplete) and are usually treated by fixation — cancellous screws or a dynamic hip screw.
  • Types III and IV are displaced and typically treated by arthroplasty — hemiarthroplasty in the frail or cognitively impaired, total hip replacement in the active elderly — with cemented stems allowing immediate weight-bearing.
  • Medical picture: the classic fragility fracture of an elderly woman after a trivial fall; in Indian practice expect osteoporotic bone, comorbid diabetes or hypertension, and often a delay before admission.
  • Pre-operative medical context: note comorbidities, American Society of Anesthesiologists grade, frailty and nutritional status, and medications (anticoagulants, steroids) — and remember this same fall may reflect a FRAX-level osteoporotic risk to address after the hip heals.
  • Pre-operative cluster 1 — function and cognition: pre-injury mobility level, independence in activities of daily living, and cognitive state (delirium risk predicts rehabilitation success more than the fracture pattern does).
  • Pre-operative cluster 2 — regional examination: the injured hip held in shortening and external rotation, pain, skin integrity over the heel and sacrum (pressure ulcers begin in the first hours on the ward), bilateral hip range of motion and strength as the patient's own baseline, and peripheral pulses.
  • Pre-operative cluster 3 — cardiorespiratory: chest expansion, breath sounds, and baseline effort tolerance (elderly supine patients decondition within days).
  • Pre-operative cluster 4 — teaching: deep-breathing and incentive spirometry, ankle pumps and circulation exercises, log-rolling technique, and rehearsing the first transfers, so post-operative day is not the first teaching day.
  • Post-operative assessment — general: vital signs, pain score, wound and dressing, drain if present, hydration, and a delirium check.
  • DVT screen: daily calf circumference and tenderness — calf pain on dorsiflexion alone is unreliable, so examine for swelling, warmth and circumference difference; remember pharmacological prophylaxis is the main protection.
  • Post-operative by fixation: after internal fixation, weight-bearing is often restricted (touch or partial) until union is shown radiographically at about six to twelve weeks, and assessment focuses on protecting the fixation while maintaining mobility.
  • After cemented arthroplasty, weight-bearing as tolerated usually begins day one, and assessment focuses on the dislocation precautions of a posterior approach — no hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation — while an anterolateral approach relaxes these.
  • Then measure: hip range of motion, abductor and quadriceps strength, sitting and standing balance, and gait with the correct aid — frame first, then stick.
  • Re-assess daily, because a post-operative hip deteriorates fast when it is not looked at.
  • Complications to screen every session: deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism (sudden dyspnoea is an emergency), wound infection, dislocation of an arthroplasty (shortened, internally rotated limb after an awkward movement), avascular necrosis and non-union after fixation, and pressure ulcers plus chest infection from immobility.
  • Outcome measures, named: the Harris Hip Score (100 points — 44 for pain, 47 for function, 4 for absence of deformity, 5 for range of motion), complemented by the timed up-and-go test and an activities-of-daily-living scale.
  • Rehabilitation phases: bed mobility and breathing on day zero; sitting and transfers day one; standing and walking with a frame days two to three; progression to a stick and stairs within the first fortnight; then strengthening of abductors and quadriceps, balance re-education and endurance.
  • Discharge planning: most Indian homes have floor-level toilets, squatting baths and possibly stairs — teach the patient and family accordingly, supply a raised toilet seat if needed, train a caregiver in safe handling, and arrange follow-up for osteoporosis management, because the fracture that predicts the next fracture is this one.

Garden I–II undisplaced → fixation; III–IV → arthroplasty; cemented stem = weight-bearing day one. Posterior precautions: no flexion beyond 90°, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation. Harris Hip Score: 44 pain + 47 function + 4 deformity + 5 motion = 100.

Sources
  • Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL — Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures (ref 16): neck of femur management and rehabilitation.
  • Maxey L, Magnusson JA — Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient (ref 13): post-operative hip protocols.
  • Garden RS — J Bone Joint Surg Br, 1961: the classification of femoral neck fractures.
  • Harris WH — J Bone Joint Surg Am, 1969: the hip rating score.
  • Kanis JA et al. — Osteoporos Int: FRAX and fracture-risk context.
