A muscle contraction where the muscle works but does not change length — no joint movement.
Isometric exercise
Muscle contraction without joint movement or change in muscle length - the first-line method in the healing phase because it protects the fracture site while preventing atrophy.
Hold 6-10 s, repeat ~10, always within pain limits - and no breath-holding.
Isometric strength
Force produced without movement, e.g. pushing against a fixed object.
Isotonic
A muscle contraction where the muscle changes length and a joint moves.
IVDP
Intervertebral disc prolapse: displacement of nucleus pulposus through a weakened annulus, most often postero-laterally where the annulus is thinnest and the posterior longitudinal ligament is weakest - hence L4-L5 and L5-S1 roots are the classic victims.
Expand the abbreviation at first use in your script - then say WHY postero-lateral: weakest zone + ligament anatomy. Two marks hidden in those two clauses.
IVDP
Intervertebral disc prolapse — a slipped disc pressing on a nerve root.
joint play
The involuntary accessory movements of a joint - roll, spin, glide, traction and compression - that must occur for full voluntary range to be possible.
Assess in the loose-packed position and always compare sides; a firm end-feel with restricted glide means mobilise, a spongy one means stabilise.
Joint protection
Techniques and habits that reduce strain on an arthritic or healing joint.
Kinematics
The study of movement itself — positions, angles, speeds — without the forces.
Kinesio taping
Elastic tape applied to the skin to support tissue and influence movement.
kinesiophobia
Excessive fear of physical movement resulting from a belief that movement will cause pain or re-injury, and a key driver of avoidance and deconditioning after surgery.
Link it straight to the fear-avoidance cycle in any post-operative question — belief, then avoidance, then stiffness, then more pain.
Kinesiophobia
A specific fear of movement or re-injury.
Kinetics
The study of the forces that produce movement.
Knee OA & load
Tibiofemoral compression is roughly 3–4× body weight in stair descent and rising from a chair; obesity multiplies cumulative cartilage loading over ~5000+ steps/day.
Quote the multiplication factor — a bare 'obesity loads the knee' statement earns half.
KOOS
The Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, a 42-item questionnaire with five subscales (symptoms, pain, activities of daily living, sport and recreation, and knee-related quality of life) scored 0 to 100 with higher scores meaning better function.
Contrast its direction with WOMAC, where higher means worse - the reversed scoring is the examiner's favourite trap in outcome-measure questions.
KOOS
Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score — a knee-specific questionnaire.
Kyphosis
An excessive forward rounding of the upper back.
Labrum
A fibrocartilaginous ring around the rim of the glenoid (and acetabulum) that deepens the socket, increases the articular surface and adds suction-stability; tears (SLAP lesions) cause painful clicking and instability.
One sentence: 'the labrum converts a flat into a cup' - then SLAP as the clinical hook.
Lachman test
The most sensitive clinical test for anterior cruciate ligament rupture, performed with the knee at 20 to 30 degrees of flexion and an anterior drawer force applied to the tibia.
Examiner's tip: quote sensitivity about 0.85 and specificity about 0.94, and always comment on the end-feel, which is soft or absent in a torn ligament.
Lactate threshold
The intensity at which lactate begins to build up faster than it can be cleared.
Laslett cluster
Five sacroiliac pain-provocation tests - distraction, compression, thigh thrust, sacral thrust and Gaenslen's - in which three or more positives identify the sacroiliac joint as the pain source.
Three of five is the number; motion tests like the stork test look impressive but are unreliable, so stake the diagnosis on provocation, not movement.
LBP
Low back pain.
LCL
Lateral collateral ligament — the ligament on the outer side of the knee.
LEFS
Lower Extremity Functional Scale — a questionnaire for lower-limb function.
level of evidence
A graded rank, typically 1 to 5, describing how well a study design protects against bias, with systematic reviews of RCTs at the top.
Pair the level with quality — a poorly conducted RCT does not outrank a well-run cohort study; saying so earns nuance marks.
Lever
A rigid bar that turns about a pivot to transmit force.
Likelihood ratio
How much a test result changes the odds of having a condition.
Likert scale
An ordered set of graded responses to a statement, typically from strongly disagree to strongly agree, used to quantify attitudes and perceptions.
Say 'ordered categories' not 'equal intervals' — treating Likert items as ratio data is the statistical sin viva examiners wait for.
Limb-salvage surgery
Wide tumour resection with endoprosthetic reconstruction, preserving the limb (vs amputation); rehabilitation follows prosthetic-fusion and quadriceps-extensor-mechanism considerations.
Post-op loading rules come from the surgeon's protocol - write that, do not improvise.
Lordosis
An excessive inward curve of the lower back.
Low-level laser therapy
Photobiomodulation (820-904 nm) with non-thermal effects on cell metabolism - modest evidence for pain in tendinopathy; dosage in joules/cm2.
Modest evidence - phrase it exactly that way in an evidence-based answer.
lower cross syndrome
Janda's pattern of tight iliopsoas, rectus femoris and thoracolumbar erector spinae with weak gluteus maximus, gluteus medius and deep abdominals, producing an anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar hyperlordosis.
A positive modified Thomas test plus a Trendelenburg lurch in the same patient is bedside confirmation - quote both in the answer.
LSI
Limb Symmetry Index — compares the injured side with the uninjured side as a percentage.
lumbosacral orthosis
A lumbosacral orthosis is a prescribed spinal support that controls motion between the lumbar spine and sacrum using rigid panels and a closure system.
For an L2-L3 lesion add the level-specific point: the orthosis must extend thoracically (TLSO logic) because a standard lumbosacral belt cannot control an upper lumbar segment.
Lx
Lumbar — the lower back region of the spine.
Lysholm score
An 8-item knee scoring scale (limp, support, locking, instability, pain, swelling, stairs, squatting) scored 0 to 100, originally for ligament injuries.
Quote that it pairs with the Tegner 0-10 activity scale - one measures how the knee feels, the other what the patient can do.
Maitland grades
A five-grade scale of oscillatory joint mobilization, from grade I small-amplitude at the start of range for pain, up to grade V a small-amplitude high-velocity thrust at the end of range.
Pair each grade with its stage of adhesive capsulitis — grade I–II for the painful freezing stage, sustained grade III–IV for the stiff frozen stage.
Malunion
A fracture that heals in a poor position.
Manipulation
A small, quick, controlled thrust to a joint.
Manual muscle grading
Grading strength from 0 (none) to 5 (normal) by hand.
Manual therapy
Skilled hands-on techniques such as mobilisation and manipulation.
MCID
Minimal clinically important difference — the smallest change in a score a patient perceives as meaningful, beyond measurement error.
Quote SPADI MCID of roughly 8 to 13 points and always pair it with the MDC, which is about 18.
MCID
Minimal clinically important difference — the smallest change in a score that a patient actually notices as worthwhile.
McKenzie method
A system of repeated movements and postures used mainly for spine pain.
MCL
Medial collateral ligament — the ligament on the inner side of the knee.
MDC
Minimal detectable change — the smallest change that is larger than measurement error.
Mean
The arithmetic average of a set of values.
Median
The middlemost observation of ranked data, with half the values below and half above it, making it the summary of choice for ordinal and skewed data.
Report it with the interquartile range, and compute one tiny live example — examiners love a candidate who can actually find a median.
Median
The middle value when values are put in order.
MET
The metabolic equivalent of task — one MET is resting metabolic rate, about 3.5 ml of oxygen per kg of body weight per minute.
Memorise everyday values — brisk walking about 4 METs, slow jogging about 7 — Indian examiners love applied MET arithmetic.
MET
Metabolic equivalent of task — 1 MET is the body's resting energy use; activity is measured in multiples of it.
Metacognition
The learner's awareness and regulation of their own thinking, placed at the top of the knowledge dimension in the revised Bloom's taxonomy.
Name it as the fourth knowledge dimension — most candidates stop after listing the six cognitive verbs.
MFR
Myofascial release — slow sustained pressure to free tight fascia and muscle.
Mill's test
Test for tennis elbow in which passive wrist flexion with the elbow extended and forearm pronated stretches the common extensor origin and reproduces lateral epicondyle pain.
Remember it is a stretch test while Cozen's is a resistance test - naming that contrast earns the interpretation mark.
Miller's pyramid
A four-tier model of clinical ability that rises from knows, to knows how, to shows how, to does.
Say the apex — does — is judged only at the patient's side, by workplace-based assessment, never by viva.
mitochondrial biogenesis
The growth and multiplication of mitochondria within muscle fibres, driven by PGC-1alpha signalling in response to endurance training.
Quote it as the dominant adaptation of endurance training, then contrast with hypertrophy to show you are not confusing training types.
MMT
Manual muscle testing — grading a muscle's strength by hand against resistance.
Mobilisation
Slow, graded passive movement of a joint to improve movement or reduce pain.
Mode
The most frequently occurring value.
Moment arm
The perpendicular distance from a joint to the line of action of a force.
Momentum
The quantity of motion of a moving body, mass times velocity.
Motivational interviewing
A counselling style that helps a patient find their own reasons to change.
Motor control
How the nervous system plans and executes movement.
Motor point
The skin site where an electrical stimulus excites the underlying nerve or neuromuscular junction at the lowest current intensity.
Place your active electrode over the motor point — maximum contraction for minimum current is a favourite viva answer.
Motor unit
An anterior horn cell, its axon and all the muscle fibres it supplies — the smallest unit of force the nervous system can switch on.
In viva questions define it this way, then add Henneman's size principle — small units first, big units for heavy loads — for the extra mark.
Motor unit
One motor nerve cell and all the muscle fibres it supplies.
MRC grade
Medical Research Council muscle-strength grade, from 0 (no contraction) to 5 (normal).
MRC grading
The Medical Research Council 0 to 5 scale of voluntary muscle contraction, in which grade 3 means full range against gravity and grade 5 means normal power against full resistance.
Grade 3 is the pivot of the whole scale - movement with gravity eliminated versus against gravity decides the orthosis and the surgical referral.
Multidisciplinary team
A group of different professionals working together on a patient's care.
Muscle fibre types
Slow (type I) fibres resist fatigue; fast (type II) fibres produce quick, powerful force.
muscle synergy
A muscle synergy is a fixed grouping of muscles that the nervous system activates together as one functional unit to produce a movement.
The exam-relevant synergies are ankle, hip and stepping strategies — listing all three in the correct order of perturbation size earns the postural control marks.
Muscle tone
The slight, ongoing tension in a resting muscle.
MWM
Mobilisation with movement — a manual glide applied while the patient performs the painful movement.
Myelopathy
A problem in the spinal cord itself, often causing clumsy hands and unsteady walking.
myofascial force transmission
The passage of muscle force to bone and neighbouring muscles through the fascial connective-tissue web rather than only along the classic tendon route.
Use it to argue that force does not respect a single origin-insertion line — a one-line definition plus one clinical example earns full marks.
Myositis ossificans
Heterotopic bone formation in muscle after trauma (classic: brachialis after supracondylar fracture); prevented by avoiding FORCEFUL passive stretching.
The sentence 'never force passive extension post-supracondylar' is exam gold.
Myotome
The muscle group supplied by a single spinal nerve segment (C4 = scapular elevation/diaphragm; C5 = shoulder abduction; L4 = ankle dorsiflexion; S1 = plantarflexion).
Anchoring each root to one movement is the fastest way to remember a neuro screen.
myotome
The group of muscles supplied by a single spinal nerve segment, tested clinically by resisted isometric contraction of a standard segmental movement.
Examiner's tip: ankle dorsiflexion for L4, great-toe extension for L5 and toe rising for S1 form the thirty-second lumbar screen every examiner expects by name.
Myotome
The group of muscles supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
NCS
Nerve conduction study — measuring how fast and how well a nerve carries electrical signals.
NDI
Neck Disability Index — a questionnaire scoring how much neck pain affects daily life.
Neer test
A shoulder test in which the examiner stabilises the scapula and passively flexes the internally rotated arm, compressing the subacromial contents under the coracoacromial arch.
Examiner's tip: quote a pooled sensitivity near 0.79 and specificity near 0.53, and conclude aloud that it is a sensitive screen that must never confirm the diagnosis alone.
Nerve conduction velocity
The speed at which a nerve carries an impulse, measured in metres per second.
Neural mobilisation
Graded movement of a nerve to reduce sensitivity and improve glide.
Neurodynamics
The clinical science of the mechanical relationship between the nervous system and its surrounding interfaces - nerves glide, slide and elongate; testing and treatment use movement (Butler, Shacklock).
Define in one line, then test names, then sliders vs tensioners - that is the answer's skeleton.
Neurodynamics
Techniques that gently move and glide nerves to improve their mobility.
Neuromatrix
The brain's own network that generates the experience of pain, not just incoming signals.
Neuromuscular control
The nervous system's smooth coordination of muscle activity for movement.
Neuropathic pain
Pain caused by damage or disease of the nervous system itself.
neutral wrist posture
Neutral wrist posture is the hand-working position of zero to minimal extension and no resting ulnar deviation, with the forearm lightly supported.
The memory hook for the exam hall: the handshake position — and pair it with the number 15 degrees of extension as the danger threshold.
NIOSH
US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health — sets lifting and workplace guidelines.
NMES
Neuromuscular electrical stimulation — a current that makes a muscle contract.
NMES instrumentation
The stimulator chain: power supply - oscillator/timer - amplifier - output transformer with charge-balanced coupling - electrodes; microprocessor-controlled in modern units.
Draw it as a block diagram; label each block with its parameter (oscillator = frequency, timer = duty cycle).
Nociception
The nervous system's detection of actually or potentially harmful stimuli.
Nociceptive pain
Pain arising from actual or threatened damage to body tissue.
Nociceptor
Free nerve endings of Aδ (sharp, fast, myelinated) and C (dull, slow, unmyelinated) fibres responding to mechanical, thermal and chemical (bradykinin, PGs, substance P) stimuli.
Aδ = first pain, C = second pain — the two-pain distinction is a free mark.
Nociplastic pain
Pain arising from altered pain processing without clear tissue or nerve damage.
Nominal scale
A scale that names categories without any order, such as blood group.
Non-maleficence
Primum non nocere - the obligation to avoid harm, including harm from overtreatment, forceful manual therapy or neglect of red flags.
Pair it with beneficence and give one physiotherapy example of each.
Non-parametric test
A statistical test that makes no assumption about the data's distribution.
Non-union
A fracture that fails to heal.
Normal distribution
The bell-shaped spread of values that many biological measures follow.
normality assumption
The requirement that data follow an approximately Gaussian distribution before a parametric test may be used.
Name an actual check — Shapiro-Wilk, or eyeballing the histogram and Q-Q plot — to show you verify it, not just recite it.
NPRS
Numeric Pain Rating Scale — the patient rates pain from 0 (none) to 10 (worst).
Null hypothesis
The statistical assumption of no difference or no association between the groups being compared, which the study attempts to reject.
State H0 and H1 explicitly before naming a test — jumping straight to a test name loses the easy structural marks.
Null hypothesis
The default assumption that there is no difference or no relationship.
OA
Osteoarthritis — 'wear-and-tear' joint disease with cartilage loss.
Objective examination
The hands-on and observed part of an assessment.
ODI
Oswestry Disability Index — a questionnaire scoring how much low-back pain affects daily life.
Oedema
Swelling caused by fluid collecting in the tissues.
Oedema management
Reducing swelling using elevation, movement, compression and other methods.
Open chain exercise
An exercise where the moving limb is free, e.g. a seated leg extension.
Opponensplasty
A tendon transfer that restores thumb opposition in low median nerve palsy by rerouting a working tendon - commonly ring-finger FDS or palmaris longus - to the abductor pollicis brevis insertion.
Always write the donor and the insertion together, for example FDS of ring finger to APB - a transfer without its insertion is half a mark.
Ordinal scale
A scale that ranks order but not the exact size of the gap, such as a pain grade.
Orthosis
An externally applied device that supports, immobilises, corrects or assists a body segment - static (no joints) or dynamic (with levers/springs).
Always prescribe with: goal, position, wearing schedule and skin checks.
orthosis
An externally applied device used to support, align, prevent or correct a body segment, or to improve its function, as distinct from a prosthesis which replaces a missing part.
Examiner's tip: pair every orthosis you list with one named indication and one limitation, because examiners mark the indication and the weaning plan, not the device name alone.
Orthosis
An external device such as a brace or splint that supports or corrects a body part.
Osteoporosis
Loss of bone density that makes bones prone to fracture.
Osteosarcoma
Commonest primary malignant bone tumour of adolescence, distal femur/proximal tibia; managed with neoadjuvant chemo, wide resection (limb-salvage with megaprosthesis) and adjuvant chemo.
The adolescent-knee location sentence anchors the whole answer.
Osteotomy
Surgery that cuts and repositions a bone.
Outcome measure
A standardised score used to track a patient's progress.
Overload principle
To improve, a tissue must be worked beyond what it is used to.
Oxidative system
Mitochondrial aerobic ATP production from carbohydrate and fat; unlimited duration, the system of endurance; depends entirely on oxygen delivery.
'Endurance = oxidative capacity' is the sentence form the evaluator underlines.
Oxidative system
The aerobic, mitochondrial system that supplies energy for long-duration work.
Oxygen debt
The extra oxygen used after exercise to restore the body's resting state.
P-value
The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
Never say the p-value is the probability that the null is true — examiners set that trap every single year.
p-value
The probability of getting a result this extreme if there were truly no real effect; a small p (usually under 0.05) suggests the result is unlikely to be due to chance.
Pacing
Balancing activity and rest to avoid pain flare-ups and fatigue.
painful arc
Pain occurring between roughly 60 and 120 degrees of active abduction, typical of subacromial impingement as the rotator cuff passes under the arch.
Examiner's tip: an arc during active but not passive abduction localises the problem to the subacromial space or cuff rather than the joint itself.
Paraesthesia
Abnormal skin sensation such as pins and needles or tingling.
Parametric test
A statistical test that assumes the data follow a normal distribution.
Patellofemoral joint reaction force
The compressive force between the kneecap and thigh bone.
Patient education
Teaching a patient about their condition and self-management.
PCL
Posterior cruciate ligament — the knee ligament that stops the shin sliding backward.
Pelvic tilt
The forward or backward rotation of the pelvis.
Peripheralisation
Distal spread of symptoms away from the spine, indicating the movement/position is aggravating the nerve root — the opposite of centralisation.
See centralisation — always define both as a pair.
Peripheralisation
Pain spreading away from the spine towards a limb — a warning sign.
PFJ
Patellofemoral joint — where the kneecap meets the thigh bone.
Phantom limb pain
Pain perceived in the absent body part after amputation, driven by peripheral ectopic discharge and maladaptive cortical reorganisation.
Pair it with mirror therapy and graded motor imagery - the strongest-evidence treatments - and never call it imaginary.
Phantom limb pain
Pain felt in a limb that has been amputated.
phase duration
The time duration of one phase of the electrical waveform, measured in microseconds.
Do not confuse it with pulse duration; the charge delivered per phase is what actually decides nerve or muscle activation.
Phases of healing
Haemostasis/inflammation (0-5 days), proliferation (5 days-3 weeks, fibroblast/collagen), remodelling (3 weeks-12+ months, collagen maturation along load lines).
Every treatment choice in this paper is justified by naming the phase it suits.
Phenomenology
Qualitative design exploring the LIVED EXPERIENCE of a phenomenon (e.g., the experience of chronic low-back pain).
One line + one example is enough; depth comes from naming analysis and trustworthiness.
Phonophoresis
Driving medicine into tissue using ultrasound.
Phosphagen system
ATP + creatine phosphate anaerobic pathway: powers maximal bursts for ~6–10 seconds (jump, sprint start, single lift). No oxygen used, no lactate made.
Every power-training justification starts with these 10 seconds — memorise the number.
Phosphagen system
The immediate energy system using ATP and creatine phosphate for short, maximal bursts.
PICOT question
A focused clinical question in five parts: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Time - the starting point of every evidence search.
Write one full example question; examiners award the worked example, not the acronym alone.
Pilot study
A small-scale preliminary run of the main study that tests the RESEARCH PROCESS (recruitment, protocol, instruments, sample-size inputs) - not the hypothesis.
Say it tests feasibility, never the effect; that single sentence anchors the whole answer.
Pilot study
A small trial run to test the methods before the main study.
Pivot shift
A dynamic subluxation and reduction of the lateral tibial plateau under the femur in an ACL-deficient knee, felt as a clunk during flexion-rotation.
In the exam, describe the mechanism before naming the test — femoral internal rotation over a fixed tibia is the sentence that scores.
pivot shift
A dynamic rotatory test that reproduces the subluxation and reduction of an anterior cruciate deficient knee as it moves from extension into flexion under a valgus load.
Examiner's tip: it is the most specific knee test, near 0.98, but needs a relaxed patient, so say it can never be the first test you perform in the sequence.
Placebo
An inactive treatment given for comparison with the real one.
Plumb line
A vertical reference line dropped from a fixed bony point, used in posture and spinal assessment to judge alignment against gravity.
Photograph the patient beside a plumb line before any measurement — it is the cheapest objective record of curvature change between visits.
PNF
Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation - diagonal-pattern strengthening and stretching using proprioceptive inputs: contract-relax, hold-relax, rhythmic stabilisation.
Name one technique and its clinical use (contract-relax for capsule-limited ROM).
PNF
Proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation — a hands-on technique using stretch and hold patterns to improve movement.
Posterior drawer
Gold-standard test for PCL integrity in which a posterior force is applied to the proximal tibia at 90 degrees of knee flexion and posterior translation is graded off the medial tibial step-off.
Grade with the three word-pictures - plateau anterior (I), flush (II), behind the condyle (III) - and always compare the other knee first.
Posterior sag sign
Visible backward drop of the proximal tibia against the femoral condyle when the legs are held with hips and knees at 90 degrees, indicating PCL insufficiency.
It is pure observation before you touch the patient and is highly specific, so look at both knees from the side the moment the patient is positioned.
postural sway
The continuous small oscillations of the centre of pressure during quiet stance, reflecting the constant corrections of postural control.
Say sway increases after ankle injury, most with eyes closed — that sensory reweighting onto vision is the modern exam point.
Postural sway
The continuous small oscillation of the body's centre of mass over its base of support during quiet standing.
Larger or faster sway marks a falls-risk candidate — one measured line in the case sheet justifies balance training.
Posture
The position of the body and its parts relative to one another and to gravity.
Power (physics)
The rate of doing work: P = W/t = force × velocity, unit watt. Muscular power is high force produced at high velocity.
Write BOTH forms of the equation. Students who write only 'strength × speed' lose the half-mark reserved for units.
Power (statistics)
The chance a study will detect a real effect if one exists.
Precaution
A situation needing care or modification rather than outright avoidance of a treatment.
Prevalence
How many people have a condition at a given time.
Primary contact
A practitioner a patient can consult directly without first seeing a doctor.
Prognosis
The expected course and outcome of a condition.
Progression
Gradually increasing the difficulty of exercise as the patient improves.
Progressive overload
The principle of gradually increasing resistance, volume or frequency so the neuromuscular system keeps adapting instead of plateauing.
Pair it with specificity in every prescription answer — principles earn marks, exercise names alone do not.
PROM
Passive range of motion — movement produced by the therapist while the patient relaxes.
proprioception
Proprioception is the sense of joint position and movement arising from receptors in muscles, tendons, joints and skin, telling the brain where the limb is without looking.
Mention that ligament injury damages mechanoreceptors too — that is the bridge from ankle injury to balance retraining, and Verhagen's recurrence data support it.
Proprioception
The body's sense of joint position, movement and force, used for balance and control.
Proprioception & guarding
Ligaments and joint capsules are densely loaded with mechanoreceptors (Ruffini, Pacinian, Golgi-like) that reflexively switch muscles on to guard the joint — ligamentomuscular reflex.
This is the bridge from anatomy to physiotherapy: proprioceptive retraining after injury is where your marks live.
Proprioceptive training
Exercises that challenge balance and joint position sense.
Prosthesis
An artificial replacement for a missing body part, such as a limb.
Provocation test
A test that reproduces the patient's pain to help locate its source.
PSFS
Patient-Specific Functional Scale — the patient names activities they find hard and rates them.
Psychometrics
The study of the measurement properties of tests and questionnaires.
pulsed electromagnetic field
A non-thermal electromagnetic agent in which time-varying magnetic fields induce weak currents in tissues without contact, used especially for promoting bone healing.
Anchor its best evidence to delayed union, non-union and fresh fractures of long bones — a favourite one-mark question.
Q angle
The angle formed by a line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the centre of the patella and a line from the tibial tuberosity to the same point, normally about 13 to 18 degrees.
State that it is higher in females, that it directs the quadriceps pull laterally, and link it directly to patellofemoral stress.
Q-angle
The angle between the pull of the quadriceps and the patellar tendon; it is normally about 13–18 degrees.
QoL
Quality of life — a person's overall wellbeing and satisfaction with daily life.
Quadriceps active test
PCL test in which the patient contracts the quadriceps or slides the foot down the plinth at 90 degrees of flexion and the posteriorly subluxed tibia visibly relocates anteriorly.
It demonstrates why quadriceps-dominant rehabilitation works in PCL injuries - link the test finding straight to the treatment principle.
QuickDASH
A short 11-item version of the DASH questionnaire.
RA
Rheumatoid arthritis — an autoimmune disease that inflames joints.
Radicular pain
Pain travelling along the path of a nerve root, often into a limb.
Radiculopathy
A problem at a spinal nerve root causing pain, tingling or weakness along a limb.
Ramp
The gradual rise and fall of stimulation intensity at the start and end of a contraction.
Randomisation
Allocation of study participants to groups purely by chance so that known and unknown prognostic factors are balanced across arms.
Pair it with allocation concealment — randomisation without concealment is like a locked door with the key under the mat.
Randomisation
Assigning participants to groups by chance to make the groups comparable.
Rate of force development
How quickly force can be produced (N/s) — the physiological expression of 'explosive strength'; improves mainly through neural adaptations.
RFD, not peak strength, predicts fall recovery in the elderly — the best single clinical line for the power section.
Rate of force development
How quickly force can be produced — the basis of explosive strength.
Ratio scale
A scale with equal gaps and a true zero, such as weight or range of motion.
RCT
Randomised controlled trial — a study in which participants are randomly assigned to different treatments.
REBA
Rapid Entire Body Assessment, a whole-body observational tool that scores the trunk, neck and legs together with the upper limbs, force and activity, and converts them into action levels 0 to 4.
Remember its two sub-scores: A for the trunk-neck-leg block and B for the arm-wrist block; combined with force and activity they give the grand score of 1 to 15.
REBA
Rapid Entire Body Assessment — a scoring tool for whole-body work posture risk.
red flag
A clinical sign or symptom suggesting serious pathology such as fracture, malignancy, infection or cauda equina compression that demands immediate medical referral.
Examiner's tip: write a one-line red flag screen into every spinal answer: night pain, weight loss, fever, trauma, steroid use, saddle anaesthesia, bowel or bladder change.
Red flag
A historical or examination finding that suggests serious pathology such as malignancy, infection, fracture or neurological compromise and mandates referral rather than manual treatment.
Memorise the spine list - weight loss, night pain, fever, sphincter disturbance, saddle anaesthesia, progressive deficit - and state the action: stop, document, refer.
Red flags
Signs and symptoms such as night pain unrelated to position, unexplained weight loss, fever, or bladder and bowel changes that suggest serious pathology beyond musculoskeletal dysfunction.
Screen for them in the first two minutes of every history and document them — missing one is the classic exam hall blunder.
red flags
Clinical features suggesting serious pathology behind a musculoskeletal complaint - cauda equina symptoms, cancer, infection, fracture or progressive neurological deficit - that mandate urgent medical referral.
In a primary-care answer, list red flags before any treatment line; failing to screen them is the classic way to lose the first two marks.
Red flags
Warning signs that suggest serious underlying disease and need medical referral.
Red-red zone
The vascular peripheral third of the meniscus (outer rim): tears there can heal because of blood supply; red-white heals partially; the inner white-white third cannot.
The zone decides repair vs meniscectomy vs conservative - one sentence, one mark.
Referral
Sending a patient to another professional for opinion or care.
Referred pain
Pain felt away from the tissue that is actually causing it.
Referred pattern
The typical area to which pain from a structure spreads.
Reflex
An automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus.
Regression
A method for describing how one variable changes with others.
Reliability
Whether a test gives consistent, repeatable results.
Residual limb
The amputated limb stump: assess shape, length, skin, scar adherence, sensation, volume stability and soft-tissue padding over the bone end.
Ideal stump: firm, cylindrical (total-surface-bearing) or conical (patellar-tendon-bearing), healed, volume-stable by 3-6 months.
Responsiveness
Whether a test can detect real change over time.
Resting membrane potential
The steady inside-negative voltage (about minus 70 mV) across the membrane of nerve and muscle cells, maintained by the sodium-potassium pump and potassium leak channels.
Write the three ions with their directions (3 Na out, 2 K in) — the ionic basis is what separates a physiology answer from a memorised one.
Rheobase
The smallest current that will excite a tissue with a long pulse.
ROM
Range of motion — how far a joint can move in each direction.
RPE
Rating of perceived exertion — how hard the exercise feels to the patient.
RULA
The Rapid Upper Limb Assessment, a observational screening tool of McAtamney and Corlett that scores posture, force and repetition to grade upper limb musculoskeletal risk from 1 to 7.
Remember the action thresholds — a score of 3 or 4 needs further investigation, 5 or above demands prompt change.
RULA
Rapid Upper Limb Assessment — a scoring tool for posture-related risk at work.
Russian current
A burst-modulated medium-frequency current, a 2500 Hz carrier delivered in 50 bursts per second, used to produce strong muscle contractions for strengthening.
Quote the 10-second on, 50-second off duty cycle — that specific detail is the mark separator.
Russian current
A medium-frequency current (2.5 kHz) delivered in bursts to build strength.
SAID principle
Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand: tissue adapts specifically to the type of demand placed on it — hence speed training for power, volume for endurance.
Pair SAID with overload and specificity — the trio of any training-principles question.
SAID principle
Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand — the body adapts to exactly the demands placed on it.
Salter-Harris
A classification of fractures through a child's growth plate.
Sampling
Choosing which people to include in a study.
sampling frame
The complete, accessible list of every member of the target population from which the sample is actually drawn.
Point out that the frame is the weak link in India — migrants and unlisted slum dwellers — to earn the selection-bias mark.
Sarcopenia
The age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength and power that predicts falls, disability and hospitalisation in older adults.
Quote 3 to 8 percent muscle loss per decade after 30, accelerating past 60 — and add that resistance training works even in the very old.
sarcopenia
The age-related, progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength and function, roughly 3 to 5 percent of mass per decade after the third decade of life.
Pair it with dynapenia — strength falls two to five times faster than mass — and say 'power' once for chair-rise and fall recovery.
Sarcopenia
Age-related loss of muscle mass, strength and function.
Saturation
The point in qualitative sampling where new interviews yield no new themes - the stop rule for enrolment (typically 10-15 in-depth interviews).
The quantitative counterpart of power analysis - examiners love that parallel.
Scapular dyskinesis
Alteration of normal scapular position and motion during arm elevation - typically protraction, downward rotation and winging - that reduces the subacromial space.
Observe it with repeated elevation after a fatigue set in overhead athletes, not just a single raise.
scapulohumeral rhythm
The coordinated 2:1 movement pattern between glenohumeral and scapulothoracic joints that produces smooth overhead arm elevation.
After cuff repair say the ratio becomes more scapular — that single sentence shows you understand compensation, not just the number.
Scapulohumeral rhythm
The coordinated 2:1 movement of the shoulder blade and the arm during elevation.
Scar management
Caring for a healing scar to keep it soft, mobile and comfortable.
Scheuermann's disease
A structural kyphosis of adolescence produced by wedging of at least three consecutive vertebrae by 5 degrees or more each, with irregular end plates and Schmorl's nodes.
The numeric trio of three vertebrae and five degrees each, plus rigid-on-extension testing, is the mark-scoring line.
Schroth method
A physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercise system combining three-dimensional self-correction, rotational angular breathing and stabilising muscle activation in the corrected posture.
Say it in one line as elongate, de-rotate, breathe into the concavity, stabilise - four words for full marks.
Scoliosis
A sideways curve of the spine.
Scope of practice
The range of activities a professional is trained and allowed to perform.
Screw-home mechanism
The small final rotation of the knee as it straightens and locks.
SD
Standard deviation — a measure of how spread out values are around the average.
Self-management
What a patient does themselves to manage their condition day to day.
SEM
Standard error of measurement — the typical error in a single measurement.
Sensitivity
Of a test, the chance it correctly identifies people who have the condition.
SIJ
Sacroiliac joint — the joint between the base of the spine and the pelvis.
Skinfold
A pinch of skin and fat measured with callipers to estimate body fat.
Skinfold caliper
A pinch gauge that estimates body fat percentage from the thickness of subcutaneous fat measured at standard sites such as triceps, biceps, subscapular and suprailiac.
Name the Durnin-Womersley four sites and add that readings should be taken on the same side, by the same tester, in duplicate.
SLAP
A tear of the upper part of the shoulder labrum (Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior).
Slider technique
Neurodynamic mobilisation moving one joint of the nervous system while releasing the other - maximal nerve glide, minimal tension; painless and usable in irritable states.
Example: shoulder abduction with neck flexion (and reverse).
SPADI
Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (Roach 1991): 13-item self-report scale - 5 pain + 8 disability items, each 0-10, total 0-100 percent; higher = worse function.
13 items (8+5) and the 0-100 percent scoring are the two facts every examiner checks.
SPADI
Shoulder Pain and Disability Index — a 13-item questionnaire (5 pain, 8 disability) scored 0–100.
Spasticity
Velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone after an upper motor neuron problem.
Special test
A specific clinical test used to confirm or rule out a particular condition.
Specificity
Of a test, the chance it correctly identifies people who do not have the condition.
Spinal curves
Four balanced curves: cervical & lumbar lordoses (secondary, mobile) and thoracic & sacral kyphoses (primary, fixed in development).
Neutral spine = maintained lordosis with balanced curves — the goal posture for IVDP control.
Spondylosis
Age-related degeneration of the spine.
Sprain
An injury to a ligament.
Spurling's test
Cervical compression test: extend, rotate ipsilaterally and axially compress the head; reproduction of radicular arm pain is positive for nerve-root compression.
Always pair with the distraction test (relief confirms the same pathology).
Squeeze test
Compression of fibula toward tibia at mid-calf; distal pain over the syndesmosis is positive for a syndesmotic (high ankle) sprain.
One of three syndesmosis tests - say all three (squeeze, Kleiger, Cotton) for full credit.
Stance phase
The part of the gait cycle when the foot is on the ground.
Star excursion balance test
Eight-direction reach test on one leg (reduced to 3 in the Y-Balance version) quantifying dynamic postural control; compare limbs, aim for >90% symmetry.
Doubles as training and discharge criterion after ankle sprain.
Step length
The distance between one foot's heel strike and the other foot's heel strike.
steppage gait
The foot-drop walking pattern of exaggerated hip and knee flexion during swing that lifts a dorsiflexor-paralysed foot clear of the ground, often with a slapping contact.
Anchor every deviation to a gait phase — 'because tibialis anterior is silent at initial contact, the foot slaps' — and mention the AFO.
Strain
An injury to a muscle or tendon.
Stratified sampling
Dividing the population into homogeneous strata (sex, severity, age band) and randomly sampling WITHIN each - guarantees subgroup representation and improves precision.
Contrast with quota sampling (non-probability) - a favourite viva trap.
Stress-strain curve
A graph showing how a tissue stretches and finally fails under load.
Stretch-shortening cycle
A muscle lengthens quickly then shortens, storing and releasing energy (as in a jump).
Stretching
Lengthening tissue by holding or moving a joint to its end range.
Stride length
The distance covered in one full gait cycle (two steps).
Stroke volume
The volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle in one beat, which rises with endurance training to raise cardiac output.
Link it to the falling resting heart rate — say stroke volume up, resting HR down, and one adaptation mark is already banked.
Stroke volume
The amount of blood the heart pumps out with each beat.
Subjective examination
The history-taking part of an assessment — the patient's story.
Subluxation
A partial dislocation, where joint surfaces shift but still partly touch.
Superior translation
Upward shift of the humeral head relative to the glenoid during elevation when the cuff cannot hold the head centred; measured as an acromiohumeral distance decrease.
Acromiohumeral narrowing on X-ray after a cuff tear is the imaging sentence worth quoting - it proves the mechanics you just described.
Sutures
Fibrous joints between skull bones, joined by sutural ligament; nearly immobile (synarthrosis); ossify with age (synostosis).
Example question: classify suture = fibrous, synarthrosis, plane — all three labels together.
SWD
Shortwave diathermy — deep heating of tissue using radiofrequency energy.
Swing phase
The part of the gait cycle when the foot is off the ground and moving forward.
Symes amputation
Amputation by disarticulation at the ankle joint with removal of the malleoli and the heel pad sutured over the tibial end to create a durable end-bearing stump.
Recite the five advantages - end bearing, long lever arm, self-suspension, near-normal energy cost, and short-distance bare-stump walking - as one list.
Symphysis
Secondary cartilaginous joint with a fibrocartilage disc over thin hyaline end-plates on both bones (pubic symphysis, intervertebral disc); permanent, slightly mobile.
The intervertebral disc IS a symphysis — a statement examiners specifically look for in Q1.
Synchondrosis
Primary cartilaginous joint united by hyaline cartilage; usually temporary and ossifies (epiphyseal plate, first sternocostal).
Opposite of symphysis in every property — write them side by side in a comparison column.
Syndesmosis
Fibrous joint united by interosseous ligament/membrane with more fibrous tissue length than a suture — slight movement (amphiarthrosis). Classic example: distal tibiofibular syndesmosis.
Ankle syndesmosis injury = high ankle sprain; its instability after rupture of TA matters — connect topics within the paper.
Synovial fluid
A dialysate of plasma plus hyaluronic acid; ~1–3 mL in a knee; boundary lubrication of cartilage + nutrition by diffusion; pH and cell count change in effusion/inflammation.
In effusion, volume can exceed 50 mL — link to quadriceps inhibition in Q4 for cross-question credit.
Synovial membrane
Inner lining of the joint capsule (except over cartilage): type A macrophage-like cells clear debris, type B fibroblasts secrete hyaluronate-rich synovial fluid.
'Everything inside the capsule except cartilage and menisci' — the boundary definition examiners quote.
Systematic sampling
Selecting every k-th individual from a list after a random start; k = frame size / sample size.
Simple and orderly - but vulnerable to hidden periodicity in the list.
T-score
BMD expressed as standard deviations from the young-adult mean; WHO: >=-1 normal, -1 to -2.4 osteopenia, <=-2.5 osteoporosis.
With fragility fracture = severe osteoporosis; Z-score is for the young.
Talar tilt
Inversion-stress test of the calcaneofibular ligament with the foot at 90 degrees; >5-10 degrees side-to-side difference suggests CFL injury.
Do not confuse with the drawer - different ligament, different position.
Tape measure (limb girth)
Measuring the circumference of a limb to track swelling or muscle bulk.
Tender points (ACR 1990)
18 bilateral sites (9 pairs) painful to ~4 kg thumb pressure; >=11 of 18 defined fibromyalgia under ACR 1990 criteria.
Four sit in the upper trunk: suboccipital, low cervical, mid-trapezius, supraspinatus - the ones this screening question needs.
Tendinopathy
Pain and degeneration in a tendon.
TENS
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, the application of surface electrodes delivering pulsed current for analgesia, conventionally 40–80 Hz (DeLisa) up to 80–100 Hz (Indian texts) at a strong but comfortable intensity.
Give both parameter sets — conventional high-frequency and acupuncture-like 2 to 4 Hz — then state the honest Cochrane position on low back pain.
TENS
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation — a small current passed through skin electrodes mainly to relieve pain.
Tensioner technique
Neurodynamic technique lengthening both ends of the nervous system simultaneously - a stronger stretch, reserved for low-irritability patients, always short of symptom reproduction.
If you cannot state when NOT to use it, you do not know the technique.
Thematic analysis
Braun & Clarke's six-phase method: familiarisation, coding, generating themes, reviewing, defining, reporting - the commonest qualitative analysis.
List the phases in order; candidates routinely reverse the first two.
Thermotherapy
Treatment using heat.
THR
Total hip replacement — replacing the hip joint with an implant.
Tinel's sign
Reproduction of tingling or electric sensations radiating into the nerve's territory when the nerve is percussed over a tunnel or entrapment point.
At the elbow percuss the cubital tunnel for ulnar nerve and 3-4 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle for radial tunnel - the classic examiner trap versus tennis elbow.
TKR
Total knee replacement — replacing the knee joint surfaces with an implant.
Torque
The turning effect of a force about a joint, equal to force times the perpendicular distance.
TrA
Transversus abdominis — the deepest abdominal muscle, a key spinal stabiliser.
TrA & multifidus
The deep local stabilisers: transversus abdominis (corset via thoracolumbar fascia) and multifidus (segmental control). Both show inhibition and atrophy after first-episode LBP (Hides et al.).
Drawing-in manoeuvre + multifidus activation = the two exercises every examiner expects under 'methods to control posture'.
Traction
A gentle pulling force applied to the spine or a limb.
Transfer training
Practising moving safely between bed, chair, toilet and standing.
Trapezitis
Overload myalgia/trigger-point syndrome of the upper trapezius, typically from sustained static elevation during desk work - the commonest occupational neck-shoulder disorder in Indian IT professionals.
Link every ergonomic element in the answer to 'removing sustained trap elevation'.
Trendelenburg
A sign of hip-abductor weakness where the pelvis drops on the unsupported side.
Trendelenburg gait
A limp from hip-abductor weakness, with the trunk leaning over the weak side.
Trendelenburg sign
A positive finding when the pelvis drops on the unsupported side during single-leg stance, indicating weak or ineffective hip abductors on the stance leg.
Remember the weakness is on the same side as the drop, the side the patient stands on, not the lifted side.
Triceps surae
Gastrocnemius (two heads, crosses the knee) + soleus (single, deep, postural) sharing the tendo-Achilles into the calcaneus; primary ankle plantarflexor.
Gastrocnemius vs soleus flexibility is tested with knee extended vs flexed — classic practical-exam pair.
Trigger point
A hyperirritable spot within a taut band of skeletal muscle that is painful on compression and refers pain to a characteristic distant zone.
Learn the referral pattern of each common muscle - the temple and jaw referral of the upper trapezius is a favourite viva question.
Trigger point
A tight, tender knot in a muscle band that can refer pain.
Trigger point vs tender point
Myofascial trigger point: focal, taut band, referred pain pattern, relieved by local treatment. Fibromyalgia tender point: systemic, no taut band, part of a central-sensitisation syndrome.
One contrast sentence with both columns earns the differential mark.
Trustworthiness criteria
Lincoln & Guba's four rigour criteria of qualitative research: credibility (=internal validity), transferability (=external), dependability (=reliability), confirmability (=objectivity).
Write each with its quantitative equivalent in brackets - instant top-band marks.
TUG
Timed Up-and-Go: rise from a chair, walk 3 m, return, sit; >12-14 s predicts falls, and <=12 s indicates community-level ambulation.
One number, one threshold - easy, always quotable.
TUG
Timed Up and Go — timing a person standing from a chair, walking 3 m, turning and sitting back down.
Tx
Thoracic — the upper back region of the spine.
Type I error
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true — a false positive whose probability is the significance level alpha.
Call it the fooling-yourself error; at alpha 0.05 you accept a 5 per cent chance of it.
Type I error
Falsely finding an effect that is not really there (a 'false positive').
Type II error
Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false — a false negative whose probability is beta.
Link it to power of 1 minus beta and say where it lives — small underpowered studies reported as negative.
Type II error
Missing a real effect that is actually there (a 'false negative').
ULNT
Upper Limb Neurodynamic Test - a sequence of limb positions (e.g., ULNT1: abduction-ER-supination-extension-wrist extension) that progressively loads the nervous system; sensitising moves (neck side-flexion) differentiate neural from muscular origin.
Learn the ULNT1 sequence by heart - it is asked by name.
upper cross syndrome
Janda's postural syndrome of tight upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid, suboccipitals and pectorals with weak deep neck flexors, lower trapezius and serratus anterior, producing a forward head and rounded shoulders.
Draw the crossed X on a stick figure and label tight versus weak - examiners give the diagram marks before they read a word.
upper crossed syndrome
Janda's pattern of tight upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals and pectorals with weak deep neck flexors and lower scapular stabilizers, typical of forward head posture.
Draw the two crossing diagonals with tight and weak labels in your margin sketch — it turns a rambling posture answer into a diagram the examiner can mark.
Urodynamics
Bladder function studies such as cystometry, uroflowmetry and leak-point pressures that characterise the neurogenic bladder after spinal cord injury.
It protects the upper tracts from high storage pressures - say that sentence and add that it guides the clean intermittent catheterisation schedule.
Validity
Whether a test measures what it claims to measure.
VAS
Visual Analogue Scale — a 0–10 line on which the patient marks their pain level.
VAS pain
Pain rated on a visual analogue scale, usually 0–10.
Viscoelasticity
The combined fluid-like and spring-like behaviour of soft tissue.
VMO
Vastus medialis obliquus — the inner teardrop part of the quadriceps above the knee.
VO2 max
The maximum volume of oxygen the body can consume per minute during exhaustive whole-body exercise, accepted as the gold-standard index of cardiorespiratory fitness.
Anchor it with the 15 to 25 percent training gain and remember it is absolute in litres per minute and relative in millilitres per kilogram per minute.
VO2 max
Maximal oxygen uptake — the highest rate at which the body can use oxygen during exercise; the gold-standard measure of fitness.
Volkmann's ischaemic contracture
Ischaemic flexion contracture of forearm muscles after untreated compartment syndrome - the feared complication of supracondylar fracture.
Screen with the 5 Ps and pain on passive finger extension - the earliest sign.
Waist circumference
A tape measure around the waist, used to judge abdominal fat and health risk.
Warm-up
Gentle activity before exercise to prepare the body.
WHO
World Health Organization.
WHO activity guidelines
The WHO 2020 recommendation that adults do 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days, with the caveat that any activity is better than none.
Use it as the prescription anchor in any answer on physical activity promotion — it converts vague advice into numbers.
Widespread Pain Index
Count of 19 body regions reported painful by the patient (0-19), combined with the Symptom Severity Scale in ACR 2010/2016 fibromyalgia criteria.
Quote that modern criteria no longer need tender-point palpation.
Wind-up
Progressive increase in dorsal-horn neuron response to repeated C-fibre input — NMDA-receptor mediated temporal summation; basis of central sensitisation.
Pattern theory's modern descendant — connecting Goldscheider to wind-up is an examiner-pleasing bridge.
Wobble board
An unstable circular platform for balance and proprioceptive training - a progression from stable single-leg stance.
Progress surfaces: floor - foam - disc - wobble board - BOSU - perturbation.
Wolff's law
Bone remodels along the lines of mechanical stress placed on it, thickening where load is high and resorbing where load is absent.
Quote it by name and you turn a plain bone-listing answer into an examiner-pleasing one; pair it with disuse osteoporosis from immobilisation.
WOMAC
Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index — a questionnaire for hip and knee arthritis.
work hardening
A structured, work-simulated progressive conditioning program that restores a patient's physical capacity to meet the documented demands of a specific job, usually over 6 to 12 weeks.
Always name the phases with week numbers and end with a functional capacity evaluation — a program without a timeline scores as a list.
Work hardening
A structured programme to build the strength and tolerance needed to return to work.
World Physiotherapy definition
Physiotherapy is services provided only by or under the direction and supervision of physiotherapists, to develop, maintain and restore maximum movement and functional ability across the lifespan, including where movement is threatened by ageing, injury, disease or environment.
Quote it nearly verbatim in any definition question - examiners recognise and reward the official wording.
Yellow flags
Psychological or social factors (fear, beliefs, work stress) that can delay recovery from pain.
